title: Contested Governance and Civilian Prosocial Behavior: Evidence from Lab-in-the-Field Experiments in India
authors: BRANDON BOLTE, VINEETA YADAV, BUMBA MUKHERJEE
abstract: How does contested governance by states and competing armed actors affect the behavior of the governed? During civil conflicts, rebel organizations frequently provide public goods, judicial arbitration, and security, but these forms of governance often operate alongside local state institutions. Beyond avoiding violence, therefore, noncombatants must navigate the daily uncertainty of local governance by states and armed groups vying for territorial control. This, we argue, shapes their quotidian interactions with one another. Using a series of lab-in-the-field experiments and surveys from Naxal-affected Bihar, India, we find that individuals living under such contested governance exhibit greater interpersonal trust and trustworthiness and less opportunistic behavior. We propose two mechanisms to explain these patterns—fearing intra-community retaliation or substituting for the state with interpersonal reliance. Most evidence is only consistent with the latter. By connecting governance, rebellion, and social capital, this work makes important contributions toward understanding the micro-politics of local order during longstanding armed conflicts.

title: Still Instrumentally Inclusive
authors: STUART J. TURNBULL-DUGARTE, ALBERTO LÓPEZ ORTEGA
abstract: Do individuals in Western democracies shift their views on LGBT+ inclusion when exposed to opposition from Muslim out-groups? And is this “homonationalist” responsiveness stronger among anti-immigration individuals? Our article “Instrumentally inclusive […]” addressed these questions using representative data from Britain (Study 1) and crowd-sourced data from Spain (Study 2). We revisit Study 2 in response to concerns about post-stratification weighting a convenience sample and erroneously inconsistent use of robust standard errors. Varying population reference parameters, weight caps, variance estimators, subgroup definitions, and covariate adjustments, we find strong support for the original findings. Neither reasonable alternative weighting schemes nor corrected variance estimators substantively change the results. In fact, the originally published point estimates are equal to or smaller than the median across alternative specifications. Consistent with the Article, we find that treatment increases support for LGBT+ inclusion in Spain, without consistent identifiable variation by immigration attitudes.

title: A Democratic Theory of Labor Unions
abstract: Recently, political theorists have been increasingly concerned with the implications of democratic values for work. This article contributes to these debates by examining the main vehicle through which workers, historically, have sought democracy at work: the labor union. The article defends a vision of economic democracy that arises from the practice of labor unions. It then emphasizes the distinctive features of labor unions that make them potential vehicles for democracy in other domains. Labor unions are particularly important means of advancing democratic values for three reasons: (1) their ability to appeal to the short- and mid-term self-interest of their members; (2) their anchor in the material reproduction of society; and (3) that they rely on attitudes of cooperation and solidarity among their members. Yet these three features also point to potential limitations of labor unions as laboratories of democracy.

title: Redistricting Reforms Reduce Gerrymandering by Constraining Partisan Actors
authors: CORY McCARTAN, CHRISTOPHER T. KENNY, TYLER SIMKO, EMMA EBOWE, MICHAEL Y. ZHAO, KOSUKE IMAI
abstract: Political actors often manipulate redistricting plans to gain electoral advantages, a process known as gerrymandering. Several states have implemented institutional reforms to address this problem, such as establishing map-drawing commissions. Estimating the impact of these reforms is challenging because each state structures its processes and rules differently. We model redistricting as a sequential game whose equilibrium solution summarizes multistep institutional interactions as a univariate score. We argue that this score measures the leeway political actors have over the partisan lean of the final plan. Our differences-in-differences analysis demonstrates that reforms reduce partisan bias and increase competitiveness by constraining partisan actors. We perform a counterfactual policy analysis to estimate the effects of enacting recent reforms nationwide. Though commissions are likely to reduce bias, reforms that restrict partisan actors in multiple ways, such as removing veto points (Michigan), are more effective than commissions where parties retain some control (Ohio).

title: Is Blood Thicker Than Water(-and-Earth)? Partisanship Geography in Imperial China and the Limits of Quantitative History
abstract: Using Wang Anshi’s Reform as a case study, Yuhua Wang’s “Blood is Thicker Than Water” ( American Political Science Review , 2022) argues that geographically dispersed kinship networks incentivize political elites to support the building of a strong state, whereas geographically concentrated kinship networks undermine state building. In this article, I improve the sample with the help of additional historical records and show that the reported correlation fails to replicate when either the control issue or the outlier issue is considered. I then propose two alternative hypotheses on the role of kinship network dispersal in Wang Anshi’s Reform, based on two common explanations of its partisanship geography in Chinese historical scholarship, that is, status competition and policy adaptiveness. After examining those hypotheses respectively, I reflect on the limits of quantitative history that this case illustrates.

title: Democratic Satisfaction and the Public Sphere
abstract: Public debate is central to most theories of democracy, yet few cross-national studies have examined its association with democratic satisfaction. This article identifies three features of national public spheres – pluralism, information, and respect – and presents annual measures of these features for 175 countries from 2000 to 2020. Among electoral democracies, pluralism remained stable, but the quality of information and the respectfulness of debate tended to decline during that period. Using data from the European Social Survey and the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems, we find that higher levels of pluralism, information, and respect correlate with greater democratic satisfaction, even after controlling for other democratic institutions, various socio-economic factors, and past levels of satisfaction with democracy. Notably, respect remains associated with higher democratic satisfaction when controlling for the other features of the public sphere. These findings call for further research into the relationship between non-electoral components of democracy and political attitudes.

title: The Equality Positions and Policies of Governments, 1970–2020: How Egalitarian Parties Evoke Equality While Evading Real Redistribution
abstract: Despite egalitarian rhetoric, governments often fail to implement redistributive policies. We argue that selective egalitarianism helps to understand this puzzle. Analysing a new dataset of 850,000 manifesto statements and equality policies in 12 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries (1970–2020), we show that even parties committed to equality avoid taxing the rich. Instead of engaging in complex top-end taxation, which is perceived as electorally risky, they pursue pre-distribution and welfare policies with less concentrated costs and complexity. Even these policies are primarily adopted if the party’s constituency is not too educated or rich to benefit from them. Our findings suggest that equality-oriented governments adopt an approach that insures the middle, buffers the poor, but spares the rich. The result is a rhetorical commitment to equality that eschews its most redistributive instrument(s). The patterns we reveal help to explain the consequential disconnect between redistributive demand and actual policy, even under ostensibly economically egalitarian governments.

title: Disproportionality in Geographic Representation
authors: Orit Kedar, Yair Amitai, Gilad Hurvitz
abstract: We theoretically develop and empirically study the concept of geographic representation. We identify an overlooked aspect of (mis)representation in electoral systems: the degree to which within parties, voters residing in some districts are overrepresented at the expense of their co-partisans residing elsewhere. Drawing on district-level data of 113 parties from twelve districted democracies, we find a substantial degree of geographic representational discrepancies within parties. Importantly, we show that the discrepancy is often accompanied by a difference in policy positions between under and overrepresented districts, making it particularly significant politically. We derive a general measure for the discrepancy between the votes a party gains and the seats it holds in different districts, namely, geographic disproportionality (GeoDisp). Unlike malapportionment, GeoDisp is party specific and draws on actual votes. Utilizing geocoded data, we find a substantial degree of geographic disproportionality, which, per our expectations, varies systematically by party.

title: The Information Paradox: Aid, Social Protection, and the Social Contract in Areas of Conflict and State Fragility
authors: Anne Della Guardia, Milli Lake, Irene Morlino
abstract: How do government-led social safety net programs in areas of violence, conflict, and state fragility shape trust in governments? Drawing on 394 qualitative interviews across twenty villages in Burkina Faso and Cameroon, we found that knowledge of governments’ roles in aid delivery programs can be a double-edged sword. While government attribution seems to improve attitudes towards governments in program sites, it widens the gap between beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries’ confidence in state institutions. Indeed, non-beneficiaries with the highest levels of information and government attribution were likely to feel more neglected by the state than those with no information. We refer to this dynamic as an information paradox, wherein information about the government’s role boosts trust in the state for some and undermines it for others.

title: Long-run effects of technological change: the impact of automation on intergenerational mobility
abstract: We examine how automation affects intergenerational income mobility. Using Swedish register data for parents and children from 1985–2019, we study how parental exposure to robots during the 1990s shaped children’s outcomes up to thirty years later. Combining occupational exposure measures with industry- and firm-level robot adoption, we find that automation reduced children’s income and upward mobility and worsened long-run labour market and educational outcomes. These effects are concentrated among low-income families and appear driven primarily by adverse parental labour market shocks and financial strain. Our findings suggest that technological change can reduce intergenerational mobility and increase long-run inequality.

title: The Value of Communication for Mental Health
abstract: Mental health disorders account for a significant share of the overall global disease burden. The economic losses from such disorders are staggeringly large, particularly in low-income countries, where people are faced with several unexpected shocks. We test whether improved communication can mitigate such mental health disorders. Partnering with a major telecommunications company, we implement low-cost communication interventions that provide mobile calling credits to a nationally representative set of low-income adults in Ghana during the COVID-19 pandemic. Individuals’ inability to make unexpected calls, need to borrow SOS airtime, and to seek digital loans decreased significantly relative to a control group. As a result, the programs led to a significant decrease in mental distress (-9.7%), the likelihood of severe mental distress by -2.3 percentage points (a quarter of the mean prevalence), and domestic violence, with null impact on overall consumption expenditure. The effects are stronger for monthly mobile credits than a lump-sum. We present evidence that improvements in both business-related services and social inclusion and/or protection are relevant explanations. Simple cost-benefit analysis shows that providing communication credit to low-income adults is a cost-effective policy for improving mental health. Communication – the ability to stay connected – meaningfully improves mental well-being and interventions about communication are particularly valuable when implemented as many installments.

title: Managerial Coordination in Decentralized Markets
abstract: Why do some buyers contract directly with producers, while others contract via an intermediary that coordinates assignments and monitors performance? We develop a repeated-game model in which intermediaries aggregate fluctuating demand, lengthening productive relationships and making cooperation easier to sustain. This benefit comes at the cost of double marginalization: an added layer of rents is needed to motivate the intermediary. The trade-off determines which buyers rely on an intermediary and which contract directly. In equilibrium, producers working through intermediaries earn lower, less variable pay but greater job security. Intermediaries expand trade, yet shift its gains from producers to buyers. Managerial coordination also promotes specialization. The framework sheds new light on professional service firms, global sourcing intermediaries, and digital matching platforms.

title: Understanding Cost Pass-Through when Prices are Dispersed
authors: Luke Garrod, Ruochen Li, Antonio Russo, Chris M Wilson
abstract: We study cost pass-through in a model of price dispersion where consumers differ in the number of firms they consider. By analysing how cost changes affect each quantile of the price distribution, we demonstrate how the effects on price dispersion and consumers’ expected purchase prices depend upon whether demand is log-concave or log-convex. We further show that consumers who consider fewer firms tend to experience a relatively smaller change to their surplus. This provides new insights into the distributional consequences of cost changes. Additionally, we examine the relation to demand shocks and the roles of competition and endogenous consideration sets.

title: Clarity of Responsibility and the Performance of Government Parties in European Second-Order Elections
abstract: European Parliament elections (EPEs) are widely regarded as second-order contests. Their perceived lower importance is expected to produce a distinct set of electoral outcomes, chief among them the proposition that governing parties lose support in EPEs relative to preceding national first-order elections (FOEs). This article examines explanatory mechanisms behind this proposition, focusing on the previously unaddressed effects of clarity of responsibility. Particular emphasis is thus given to whether the expected losses vary with government parties’ size and cabinet role, and with other factors that shape responsibility attribution, including coalition size, ministerial portfolio shares and prior government experience. In addition, I also assess whether parties providing formal external support to governments face electoral penalties in EPEs. Covering all EPEs and corresponding FOEs from 1979 to 2024, the study also examines whether the second-order model and its key mechanisms, such as election timing, have shifted over time in response to broader transformations in European politics.

title: Rival or Villain? The Evolution of Language Depicting the Opposition under Authoritarianisation
authors: Alper H. Yagci, Cemal Yılmaz, Uzay Çetin
abstract: Discursive attacks towards the opposition are often a harbinger of polarisation, democratic backsliding and authoritarianism. We study the evolution of negative language about the opposition in Turkey under Erdoğan, a pioneering case of democratic backsliding. We distinguish between two types of negative language: a valid competitor – ‘rival’ – versus an enemy that needs to be destroyed – ‘villain’. We leverage machine learning to examine every opposition-related sentence in two major newspapers from 2009 to 2022. Our data allow us to compare the depictions of the main opposition party as a rival or villain between media outlets, before and after media ownership change, during election times and beyond. We also test how these depictions respond to currency shocks and military casualties, as the incumbents could try to contain the fallout from these adverse events by discursively attacking the opposition. We find that vilification of the opposition is driven by security challenges rather than economic troubles, which are associated with increases in rival discourse. Results also suggest that political competition can appear unrepresentatively civil precisely during election periods, as an already polarising incumbent may try to present himself in a more reconciliatory light during the campaign period.

title: Migration and the Politics of Integration. By KarinBorevi and AyhanKaya, Cham, Switzerland: Springer, IMISCOE Research Series, 2026. 127 pp. Open Access (paperback). ISBN : 978‐3‐03‐221785‐1 ( ebook )
Beyond Divided Loyalties: How Transnational Family Ties Enhance Political Trust in High‐Emigration Countries
authors: Jing Zhang, Ruiyuan Ding, Nan Zhang
abstract: Existing literature on candidates' transnational background generally associates cross‐border ties with weakened political trustworthiness, emphasizing concerns over divided loyalty and reduced commitment to domestic development. This perspective, however, overlooks contexts in which mass emigration has become increasingly common. We argue that in societies characterized by widespread emigration, transnational family ties can instead function as political assets by fostering in‐group identification and signalling shared interests with voters who have similar experiences. To test these hypotheses, we conduct a survey experiment among 1782 Venezuelan adults in July 2024. Results confirm that candidates with transnational family ties receive significantly higher trust ratings than those without such connections, and this effect is particularly salient for female candidates. These findings challenge the prevailing ‘political curse’ narrative and lead to a more comprehensive understanding of political trust in societies with high emigration rates.

title: Balancing Act: Coercion, Terrorism, and Regime Stability
authors: Allison Carnegie, Aleksandra Gracheva, Adam Lichtenheld, Dipali Mukhopadhyay
abstract: A substantial literature seeks to understand the drivers and consequences of foreign policy instruments that states employ to change the behavior of other states. We argue that this body of work—and the surrounding policy discourse—often miscategorizes or misunderstands the goals of these instruments in the important set of cases involving the threat of terrorism. We contend that the deployment of these instruments depends on the relationship between the target regime and the coercing state and the degree to which the coercing state perceives a terrorist threat emanating from the target’s territory. We develop a typology that characterizes and predicts foreign policy approaches as a function of these two concerns. We theorize that, in cases where the target regime is adversarial and where a distinct terrorist threat is perceived, the coercer employs a balancing approach. It seeks to apply enough pressure to keep the target regime weak, but not so much that the regime collapses, which could allow extremist non-state actors to assume control. We use in-depth case studies of US foreign policy in Syria and Afghanistan to contest the common narrative that sanctions fail and, instead, contend that maintaining regime limbo often serves US goals and interests as defined in the post-9/11 era.

title: Executive constraints and incumbent takeovers
abstract: This paper provides a systematic study of how judicial and legislative constraints on the executive safeguard against incumbent-driven regime transitions and argues that the relationship, across the regime-type spectrum, should take the shape of an inverted U. The basic argument is based on opportunity and incentive. In regimes with high levels of constraints, incumbents are inhibited by their institutions from taking over, whereas incumbents in regimes with very low levels of constraints provide no incentive for such moves. However, in regimes with medium levels of constraints, the constraining institutions restrict the incumbent enough to incentivize takeover whilst remaining insufficient to curtail them. This relationship is examined using newly available data on incumbent-induced breakdown, spanning over 2,000 regimes. Different operationalizations of the dependent variable are employed to sufficiently account for the incremental nature of incumbent takeovers. A series of TSCS Logit and LPM models find consistent and largely robust support for the hypothesis.

title: The effects of population settlements and territorial labeling on domestic audience: Evidence from Israeli settlements in the West Bank
abstract: States trying to absorb previously external territories under dispute need to convince their national community that the newly acquired territory is an indivisible part of the homeland, important for national security, identity, and prosperity, and is generally worthy of incorporation even at a cost of a protracted conflict. Two strategies that states use to this end are territorial labeling, which means assigning a name to the territory that evokes intrinsic ties to the nation's history and populating the acquired territory with members of the national community (population settlements). To date, no empirical study has evaluated the impact of these two strategies. Using an original survey experiment in the case of Israel, we test the impact of territorial labeling and population settlements on the propensity of Israeli Jews to view the territories Israel conquered from Jordan in the 1967 war (West Bank/Judea and Samaria) as tied to their homeland, important for economic prosperity and national security, and on support for annexation and continued population settlements. We find that territorial labeling is consequential for all our outcomes of interest, whereas the impact of population settlements, specifically the demographic concentration of conationals, is on perceptions of connection to historic homeland and security importance, with no observed effect on policy preferences. These findings have theoretical implications for our understanding of how national territories are socially constructed and made seem more indivisible, demonstrating specifically the impact of symbolic-discursive practices and tangible, material changes on territorial attachments and policy preferences in territorial conflicts.

title: Christopher A. Sims (1942–2026): Paradigm-shifting macroeconomist and econometrician
abstract: Christopher A. Sims, who died on March 14, 2026, left behind an indelible mark on macroeconomics and econometrics. His Nobel Prize winning research reshaped the paradigm for empirical macroeconomics, creating a rigorous and flexible framework for inferring the effects of macroeconomic policies. He also made important contributions to time series forecasting, Bayesian econometrics, factor modeling, approximation theory, and models of monetary and fiscal policy. Few academics have had as direct an impact on the work of central banks throughout the world. A frank and generous mentor with numerous students, Chris’s impact extends well beyond his published papers.

title: Parenthood decisions in uncertain times: Experimental evidence from four countries
authors: Arnstein Aassve, Letizia Mencarini, Chen Peng, Samuel Plach, Alonso Román Amarales, Maria Letizia Tanturri
abstract: Fertility rates are declining across much of the globe, yet the forces driving this decline have become increasingly complex, and classic theories have become less adequate to explain recent trends. While economic and gender-related explanations have long dominated fertility research, emerging global uncertainties, such as climate change, democratic backsliding, economic crises, and regional conflicts, may also shape how individuals evaluate childbearing. In addition to the more classical factors, this cross-national study examines how macrolevel uncertainties influence perceptions of fertility intentions in Italy, Argentina, the United States, and Germany. These countries offer distinct fertility trajectories and face unique combinations of sociopolitical and environmental challenges. Using a conjoint experiment, we examine how individuals evaluate, across hypothetical scenarios, their intention of having a child under varying household, policy, and macrolevel conditions. Across all four countries, material security remains central: household income is the strongest predictor of fertility intentions, with homeownership and childcare playing smaller roles. At the same time, perceptions of macrolevel stability, including expectations about climate conditions, economic prospects, democratic functioning, and peace, exert substantial and meaningful effects, comparable to homeownership and childcare provision but more pronounced than those associated with gender-role arrangements. Cross-country differences show that macroeconomic stability and climate change are most consequential in Argentina, while in the United States respondents are less responsive to geopolitical conflict. These findings show that individuals evaluate childbearing not only through their immediate circumstances, but also through expectations about broader societal futures, highlighting the importance of incorporating macrolevel uncertainty when explaining contemporary fertility decline.

title: Treating language contact as normal: Coalescent-theoretic modeling of the prehistory of the Bantu language family
authors: Patrícia Santos, Andrea Benazzo, Silvia Ghirotto, Igor Yanovich
abstract: The Bantu language family of sub-Saharan Africa is among the largest in the world by the number of languages, by geographical extent, and by the number of speakers. The expansion of the Bantu languages is an important example of large-scale language-family expansions in the history of humankind. To learn the early prehistory of the Bantu language family, one needs to disentangle the signal of the original splits and diversification from that of the subsequent language contact, known to be strong in the Bantu languages. We introduce a coalescent-theoretic model to computationally study the prehistory of the Bantu family. Our model treats language contact as a norm rather than a rare exception, in contrast to earlier computational work. Applying Approximate Bayesian Computation, we show the rates of both language change and language contact to have been so high within the Bantu family that the signal of the original diversification has been largely erased in the currently available Bantu lexical data.

title: Can stimulating ownership increase fertility: Evidence from housing interventions in China
authors: Xin Zhang, Dongxue Wu, William A.V. Clark
abstract: Declining fertility and the emergence of very low TFR’s in the Asian economies has increased the focus on how to change the direction of the fertility trend. Several countries in Europe and Asia have explored a variety of stimulus packages to increase the overall TFR. In this research we review those policies and examine one of those interventions which has the potential to stimulate fertility—the role of access to housing. The core of housing approaches to stimulating fertility is to make housing more accessible and to use various forms of credit assistance with the aim of making ownership easier and more attractive to young families. The research asks how effective are these approaches to reversing the decline in fertility? And, are they a solution to very low fertility? The results provide some evidence that the focus on housing stimulus packages may increase fertility although most successfully for socioeconomically advantaged households.

title: Psychological inoculation against climate doom
authors: Rachel O’Boyle, Tyler Shores, Sander van der Linden
abstract: Individuals encounter “climate doom,” extreme portrayals of climate change, on social media. While climate doom may be intended to motivate action, it may also be perceived as manipulative or elicit hopelessness. Yet, no research has examined whether psychological inoculation helps to improve recognition of climate doom or influences engagement with it on social media. In this preregistered study ( n = 521), we tested whether inoculation improves discernment of climate doom and influences engagement with it by collecting behavioral data using a social media simulator. We find that inoculation substantially improves discernment of climate doom and that this is due to increased perceived manipulation of doom messaging specifically ( d = 0.68). There was no interaction between the inoculation condition and political leaning and while higher perceived manipulation of doom content predicted lower behavioral intentions, inoculation did not moderate this relationship. Inoculation increased engagement, particularly disliking and flagging of doom content, and decreased sharing. Overall, our results should lead climate communicators to reconsider doom messaging as a mobilization strategy and demonstrate that inoculation is an effective tool for increasing recognition of, and critical engagement with, climate doom across the political spectrum.

title: A demographic theory of similarity-biased social learning
authors: Alejandro Pérez Velilla, Paul E. Smaldino
abstract: We develop a demographic theory of similarity-biased social learning that formalizes our understanding of when and why individuals should preferentially copy others that look or act like them. We build an evolutionary model in which individuals can either learn on their own or copy others from a demonstrator pool that contains varying proportions of in-group and out-group members, and where group tags can be more or less informative about local knowledge. We find that where social learning becomes common, selection favors copying biases that track the direction of informational advantage—toward the group that tends to be better adapted to local conditions, including an antisimilarity bias when tags are negatively associated with local correctness (as may be the case for some immigrant communities). We also find conditions in which a similarity bias can stabilize social learning when such learners are already common, but not when they are rare, with implications for the role of group identities in cultural evolution. We discuss implications for understanding parochialism as risk aversion, majority–minority dynamics, the sociology of immigration, and the lasting impacts of colonialism.

title: ICE arrests, 2015–2026: Variation in targeting, method, and geography
authors: Chloe N. East, Caitlin Patler, Elizabeth Cox
abstract: We analyze and decompose administrative data on all 1.6 million US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests from October 2015 to March 2026. Our results reveal that the reality of immigration enforcement diverges sharply from the public narrative that ICE arrests are necessary to protect public safety by removing people who commit crimes: Although arrests spiked at the outset of both Trump presidencies, the share of arrested individuals with criminal convictions fell significantly, with especially marked declines in 2025. A shift in ICE tactics partly explains this pattern, but even conditional on tactic, the share with a criminal conviction declined as arrests rose. Moreover, we find substantial geographic heterogeneity in ICE methods, despite nearly universal declines in the criminal conviction rate. Our findings provide important evidence for policymakers, the general public, and researchers studying this period of immigration policy.

title: Developmental changes in memory structure and precision alter the use of retrieved episodes during decisions for reward
authors: Nora C. Harhen, Aaron M. Bornstein, Catherine A. Hartley
abstract: Most widely studied option evaluation strategies rely on knowledge accumulated across repeated experiences. But how should options be evaluated in unfamiliar environments, in which knowledge is sparse? In these situations, how do decision makers make efficient use of limited past experience to guide their choices? One possible strategy is episodic sampling, in which a decision maker retrieves a small number of past decisions from memory to estimate the value of present options. By virtue of their age, children and adolescents have less experience than adults, making episodic sampling a particularly useful strategy for them. At the same time, the effectiveness of episodic sampling derives from memory’s precision and context sensitivity—properties that continue to develop into adolescence and young adulthood. This tension raises a key question: are developmental differences in episodic memory associated with differences in episodic sampling? To address this question, 106 participants, ages 8 to 25, completed a 2-d choice task that dissociated the influence of a single episodic memory from the influence of multiple episodes sharing a common context. At all ages, single episodes biased choices. But, only adults were sensitive to the broader evoked context. Further clarifying the relationship between episodic memory and decision making, differences in memory precision predicted differences in episodic sampling, even after taking into account age, while episodic sampling, in turn, accounted for individual differences in forward planning. Together, these findings suggest that episodic memory guides decision making throughout development, but the character of its influence evolves as memory becomes more precise and richly structured.

title: The social-class gap in negotiation: Lower-class individuals negotiate less and face more backlash
authors: Ying Lin, Jackson G. Lu, Michele J. Gelfand
abstract: Economic inequality has widened considerably in the United States and globally, raising pressing questions about the mechanisms that reproduce social stratification. One prominent manifestation of this inequality is the “class ceiling” in organizations: individuals from lower social classes earn less and advance more slowly than their higher-class counterparts, even with comparable credentials. We identify a crucial behavioral pathway contributing to this class ceiling: a social-class gap in the propensity to negotiate. We propose that lower-class individuals are less likely to initiate negotiations than their higher-class counterparts, a pattern that can compound economic disadvantage over time. Across four studies (total N = 10,211)—including a nationally representative sample of employees (Study 1), a sample of business school students (Study 2), a field study of an online labor market (Study 3), and a survey study of workplace negotiations and career outcomes (Study 4)—we find consistent evidence for this gap. This gap is partially explained by lower-class individuals’ reduced sense of power and heightened concerns about social backlash. Additionally, Study 5 ( N = 1,133) finds that such concerns may be justified: an experiment with human resources (HR) professionals shows that identical negotiation requests elicit stronger social backlash when initiated by lower-class (vs. higher-class) individuals. Together, these findings reveal a pernicious double bind for lower-class individuals: remaining silent perpetuates economic disadvantage, yet initiating negotiation exposes them to greater social penalties. Addressing this double bind is critical for ensuring that negotiation serves as a vehicle for upward mobility rather than a gatekeeper of privilege.

authors: Katherine A. Thomas, Thomas B. Storrs, Wenfei Xu, Jacob W. Faber

title: Whose China Shock? Partisanship, import exposure, and trade rhetoric in the US Senate
abstract: Trade among major powers is never purely economic; it is also a site of political conflict over blame, threat, and national interest. Why, then, do legislators facing similar trade shocks respond in such different ways? Focusing on US Senate rhetoric on trade with China between 2009 and 2023, this paper examines how partisanship conditions the translation of economic disruption into elite political speech. Drawing on sentiment analysis of Senate floor speeches and state-level measures of Chinese import exposure across two periods, it develops a partisan-conditioning argument: trade disruption acquires political meaning as parties interpret it. Democratic senators grew markedly more critical as local import exposure increased, especially under the earlier China Shock window. Republicans showed a much flatter response to early-period exposure and even a slightly positive association with later-period penetration. The China Shock left a durable mark on Senate discourse, but one structured by party, not geography alone.

title: The politics of crime prevention: Evidence from Colombia
abstract: Why do governments prevent crime in some places while neglecting others? Crime prevention policies are often viewed as too slow, diffuse, and politically intangible to generate electoral rewards. When implemented, existing research suggests they primarily serve to reward co-partisans or mobilize ideologically aligned voters. This article challenges that view by arguing that incumbents allocate crime prevention resources to electorally competitive municipalities because these investments yield electoral returns. Using detailed project-level data from Colombia, I show that national incumbents disproportionately direct crime prevention funds to municipalities where recent presidential elections were closely contested, rather than to areas with higher crime rates or strong partisan loyalties. I then show that these allocations increase the vote share of the right-wing incumbent coalition in subsequent elections. Drawing on quantitative analyses and interviews with policymakers and bureaucrats, I argue that these effects operate primarily through the visibility and attribution of crime prevention projects, particularly those aligned with right-wing issue ownership of public security.

title: Evaluations of institutional performance among adolescents: Comparing the socializing roles of schools and families
abstract: Democratic accountability requires citizens’ political trust to reflect institutional performance, making it crucial to understand what fosters such responsiveness. While existing studies suggest that education shapes evaluative attitudes, direct evidence remains limited because many analyses struggle to separate educational effects from those of parental background. This paper offers a comprehensive test of these explanations by examining adolescents within the same target grade and by assessing school-level civic education characteristics often credited with cultivating critical citizenship norms. It then compares school-level patterns with parental background to evaluate the proxy-versus-cause debate. Using data from three waves of the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study, the analysis shows that structurally low and declining institutional performance depresses political trust among adolescents. However, consistent with the education-as-proxy argument, the positive association between performance and trust is significantly stronger among adolescents with higher parental socio-economic status, while school-level civic education shows no meaningful moderating effect.

title: Who supports martial law in a democracy? Lessons from South Korea
abstract: On 3 December 2024, South Korea experienced an unprecedented political crisis when the president declared martial law. While the declaration was rapidly reversed and condemned by key democratic institutions, public opinion did not converge on rejection. Instead, support for—and tolerance of—the measure persisted among a nontrivial share of citizens. Why, in a democracy with functioning institutions, are some citizens willing to accept extraordinary executive measures? Using original nationwide survey data, this research shows that public support for martial law is strongly associated with affective polarization. Individuals who express strong partisan and leader-based affective alignment with the incumbent are significantly more likely to accept martial law, while those polarized in the opposite direction overwhelmingly reject it. The findings suggest that affective polarization can align evaluations of executive overreach with partisan loyalties, weakening normative constraints even in consolidated democracies where institutional safeguards continue to function effectively.

title: Fair reciprocity and EU law
abstract: Should all European Union (EU) citizens enjoy the same welfare benefits as nationals when they migrate within Europe? Which categories of EU migrants (workers, job-seekers and non-economically active ones) should be entitled to full equal treatment? I discuss reciprocity as a moral basis of EU law, extending White’s account of fair reciprocity to the supranational context of the EU. I suggest that the concept of workers in EU law should be reformed to account for a plurality of valuable contributions. I also discuss the implications of reciprocity in non-ideal conditions, arguing that EU migrants have a reduced contributive obligation when they face injustice in the host member state. The seriousness of such injustice may even imply lifting the contributive obligation entirely. The contributive obligation of non-economically active individuals is a duty to seek work, and I suggest it entitles them to limited equal treatment.

title: The trust in government gap: National trust, local trust, and compliance
authors: Susan Banducci, Laszlo Horvath, Daniel Stevens
abstract: According to Tang and Huhe, individuals “are nested in a multiplicity of governments,” including national and local governments, “and . . . constantly find themselves in variant relationships with government at different levels”. Yet, previous research has mostly concentrated on individuals’ assessments of national governments, or supranational organizations such as the European Union, overlooking assessments of local governments and their effects. To address this, we fielded a four-wave survey in England in 2020–2021 capturing local and national government trust, as well as contemporaneous indicators of performance across these levels of government. Disaggregating between- and within-individual explanations for variation, we find distinct influences on trust in national and local government, and that trust in local government exerts an influence on pro-social behaviour whereas national government trust does not. Importantly, for future research on political trust, our findings show that the level of government matters for both the drivers and consequences of political trust.

title: Constituent power and constituent collectives in a Union context: Deciding the futures of Scotland and the United Kingdom
abstract: Over the last few decades, interconnected debates about Scottish independence and Brexit have shaped politics in the United Kingdom and raised questions of constituent power that remain controversial both politically and theoretically. Against this backdrop, this article proposes a nuanced democratic conception of constituent power that serves as an alternative to orthodox sovereigntist accounts. This conception is theoretically more compelling and, moreover, enables fruitful engagement with contemporary constitutional controversies. By establishing a dialogue between theoretical discussion and the Scottish and UK case, the article, first, explores constituent power as one dimension of popular sovereignty and its interplay with constituted powers over time. Second, it examines how constituent collectives can and, in recent history, have become subject to contestation and change. Third, it sketches monist and pluralist conceptions of constituent power and peoples that co-exist, yet conflict within the United Kingdom, thereby mapping distinct trajectories for possible constitutional futures in a union setting.

title: American Administrative Capacity: Decline, Decay, and Resilience By M.Ernita Joaquin and Thomas J.Greitens, Cham, Switzerland: Springer, 2021. 213 pp. $97 (hardcover). ISBN : 978‐3‐030‐80563‐0
Linking Decision Roles to Knowledge Utilization in US State Governments: A Mixed‐Method Study
authors: Shuping Wang, Yuan (Daniel) Cheng, Chengxin Xu
abstract: The current movement for evidence‐based policymaking advocates the use of scientific knowledge in government. However, in practice, civil servants often prioritize different types of knowledge depending on their decision‐making roles and the context. Using survey responses from 259 civil servants across three US state governments and 36 semistructured interviews, we employ a mixed‐method approach to understand how civil servants strategically utilize various types of knowledge to meet different role requirements and decision‐making responsibilities. Consistent with our hypotheses, our findings indicate that civil servants involved in policy and legislative roles value political knowledge more, while those in contracting roles place greater importance on experiential knowledge. Contrary to our hypothesis, while civil servants in budgeting roles value political knowledge more than their counterparts in other decision roles, they show no such preference for scientific knowledge. Our qualitative interviews provide possible mechanisms for this unexpected finding.

title: The Matthew Effect in American Generosity? Philanthropic Disparities and the Role of Government Support
authors: Viviana Chiu Sik Wu, Ji Ma, Chao Guo
abstract: This study examines how economic, racial, and ecological dimensions of community disadvantage shape philanthropic donations to local human services nonprofit sectors, and whether government support mitigates these place‐based disparities. Using a novel county‐level panel dataset spanning 2000–2019, we combine descriptive analyses with mixed‐effects regression models to estimate both direct and moderating relationships. We find that per capita private donations are significantly lower in economically deprived communities and significantly higher in rural communities, while minority prominence shows no statistically significant association with private giving. While government funding crowds in private donations overall, its moderating role is context specific. Government support does not attenuate philanthropic disparities linked to economic deprivation or minority prominence, but it crowds in private donations more strongly in rural counties than in urban counties. These findings highlight the contingent role of government support and underscore the need for targeted policy strategies to address philanthropic disparities across communities.

title: Bureaucracy Remade, Citizens Reconfigured: Accountability, Digitalization, and the Transformation of Public Administration
The Rise of Midocracy: How NPM and Post‐ NPM Reform Ideas Recombine in Contemporary Public Organizations
abstract: This paper introduces and conceptualizes midocracy as an emergent organizational form in the public sector, characterized by the growth and dominance of a professionalized administrative middle layer. The study argues that midocracy draws on elements associated with both New Public Management (NPM) and post‐NPM reform agendas. While administration is essential for coordination, we show how its unchecked expansion can lead to self‐reinforcing dynamics that distance governance from core operations. Midocracy, we contend, reflects a shift from service delivery to symbolic value signaling, strategic abstraction, and polycentric goal‐setting. Our contribution is both conceptual and diagnostic, offering midocracy as a framework for understanding contemporary administrative expansion and its implications for public sector legitimacy and performance. Finally, we relate and critically examine different explanatory accounts of administrative expansion, highlighting how they interact within the dynamics of midocracy.

title: Nonpolitical Identity Signals as Information Shortcuts: Evidence from Three Experiments
authors: Levi G Allen, Wayde Z C Marsh
abstract: A rich literature has documented how voters navigate the complex information landscape by using heuristics, or “information shortcuts,” to help them make sense of the political world. Additionally, a budding line of research argues that our current polarization crisis has extended beyond just the political and now even affects the nonpolitical realm. We submit that voters may be using these nonpolitical identity signals (e.g., a candidate driving a Toyota Prius or eating at Chick-fil-A) as heuristics to make sense of the contemporary political era. Using three original survey experiments, we find that these nonpolitical identity cues are indeed used by voters as partisan heuristics, but only in the absence of political (partisan and issue) informational cues. Furthermore, we also suppress the effect of partisan identification when we provide orthogonal nonpolitical information. These findings show that nonpolitical identity items can be used by citizens as information shortcuts to help citizens navigate the complicated political waters that surround them, but that their effect in light of other pieces of information is minimal.

title: Capital Services in Global Value Chains
abstract: This paper constructs the first global dataset on inter-sectoral capital service expenditures. I use this data to disaggregate capital services and intermediate inputs in a dynamic multi-sector trade model. Steady state allocations and responses to shocks are determined by a capital-augmented global input-output matrix. Two properties of the measured network deliver larger long-run consumption gains from globalization than existing estimates, as well as larger gains in more capital-intensive countries. First, more trade-exposed sectors supply capital to more consumption-influential producers. Second, heterogeneity in the network reallocates sectoral expenditures towards producers with larger declines in capital rental prices. These reallocations raise capital incomes and lower consumption price indices.

title: Mental Models of the Stock Market
authors: Peter Andre, Philipp Schirmer, Johannes Wohlfart
abstract: Investors’ return expectations are pivotal in stock markets, but the reasoning behind these expectations is not well understood. This paper explores economic agents’ mental models of what drives returns. We survey the general population, retail investors, financial professionals, and academic experts to investigate how they forecast and explain future returns in scenarios with stale news about future company earnings. We find that investors strongly disagree in their forecasts and reasoning. Most academic experts view markets as efficient. By contrast, most households express a perspective we call “expected earnings reasoning”: they directly equate higher expected earnings with higher expected returns. Professionals are split between market efficiency, mispricing, and expected earnings reasoning. In detailed experiments, we dissect why households adopt expected earnings reasoning. We show that it arises from inattention to how stock-price changes affect investor costs — that is, how much investors must pay to acquire a claim to future cash flows — because the typical format and context of investment problems obscure these cost implications. Our results help connect a series of previously documented anomalies in expectation and trading data and highlight the importance of selective attention and context in shaping reasoning and belief formation.

title: The Transmission of Reliable and Unreliable Information
authors: Thomas Graeber, Shakked Noy, Christopher Roth
abstract: Information often spreads and influences beliefs regardless of its reliability. We show that this occurs in part because indicators of reliability tend to be lost in the process of word-of-mouth transmission. We conduct controlled experiments where participants listen to economic forecasts and pass them on through voice messages. Other participants listen either to original or transmitted audio recordings and report incentivized beliefs. Across various transmitter incentive schemes, a claim’s reliability is lost in transmission much more than the claim itself. Reliable and unreliable information, once filtered through transmission, impact listener beliefs similarly. Mechanism experiments show that reliability is lost not because it is perceived as less relevant or harder to transmit, but because it is less likely to come to mind during transmission. Evidence from our experiments, a large corpus of everyday conversations, and economic TV news shows that contextual cues can bring reliability to mind and induce its transmission, but situations in which people share information seldom contain such cues.

title: An Evaluation of Protected Area Policies in the European Union
authors: Tristan Earle Grupp, Prakash Mishra, Mathias Reynaert, Arthur A van Benthem
abstract: The European Union designates 26% of its landmass as protected areas, limiting economic development for biodiversity. We use the staggered introduction of protected areas between 1985 and 2019 to study the selection of protected land and the causal effect of protection on vegetation cover and nightlights. We find no meaningful impacts on either outcome across four decades, countries, protection cohorts, or land characteristics. These null effects are consistent with the political economy of EU land protection: weak incentives to internalize biodiversity gains, green-glow motives, and area-based targets shape local siting and stringency choices. In practice, strict protection is applied where development pressure is low–so that protection has little bite—while in high-pressure regions, protection is typically weak, imposing only limited constraints on economic activity.

title: When is Separate Sales Optimal?
abstract: This paper studies a multi-product monopolist facing a privately informed consumer with additive and type-increasing valuations. Separate monopoly pricing is robustly optimal with respect to the type distribution if and only if the marginal rate of substitution between each pair of goods is monotone. This result is obtained by extending the conventional Myersonian approach.

title: Macro Shocks and Firm Dynamics with Oligopolistic Financial Intermediaries
abstract: Motivated by a secular increase in the concentration of the U.S. banking industry, I develop a new macroeconomic model with oligopolistic financial intermediaries and heterogeneous firms. Market power allows banks to price discriminate and charge firm-specific markups, exerting greater market power over productive and more financially constrained firms. This dampens capital accumulation and amplifies the effects of macroeconomic shocks. During a crisis, banks exploit the higher share of financially constrained firms to extract higher markups, inducing a larger decline in real activity. When a large bank fails, the remaining banks use their increased market power to restrict credit supply, worsening and prolonging the downturn.

title: Churn, not crisis, for UK science
abstract: When Andy Burnham became the United Kingdom’s prime minister last week, among his first acts was to abolish the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), folding it into a new superministry for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade . The science minister, Patrick Vallance , stepped down the same day. Viewed from the United States, where the federal research system is under pressure, it may be tempting to see Britain’s reshuffle as kindred turmoil and proof that political instability is corroding science on both sides of the Atlantic. That reading would be wrong. Britain has rearranged the machinery of its science policy, not undermined its foundations. The change could sharpen the contribution of UK research to the economic renewal that Burnham has made his defining mission.

The Bio-Functional Audience: Shared Physiological Alignment to Narrative Media
authors: Ralf Schmälzle, Hee Jung Cho, Monique Mitchell Turner
abstract: Communication research into audience responses has traditionally emphasized how individual or group differences create variance in interpretation while overlooking a more fundamental phenomenon: the capacity of the same message to induce similar responses across receivers. We introduce a bio-functional definition of the audience, a temporal collective bound together by the moment-to-moment alignment of its members’ physiological responses. In a large-scale experiment ( N = 198) monitoring eye-tracking, heart rate, and electrodermal activity during a film, we mapped a processing hierarchy in which audience response alignment was strongest for gaze but also extended into downstream autonomic responses. Furthermore, a temporal manipulation of the narrative sequence abolished aligned responses, confirming that the induced audience state is driven by the message content. We conclude that messages function as alignment devices that reduce individual noise and bring distinct individuals into a shared processing state, thus providing a grounded, signal-based definition of the audience as a bio-functional entity.

title: Music Was My First Love: Biographic Resonance Makes Everyday Music Listening Meaningful
authors: Felix Dietrich, Alicia Ernst, Benedikt Rohr, Michael Scharkow, Leonard Reinecke
abstract: Despite much research on eudaimonic media experiences, little is known about how and why certain content is perceived as meaningful by certain users in certain situations. We therefore examine biographic resonance — connections between entertainment content and users’ biographic memories — during everyday music listening on Spotify and propose that memory recall, as well as its emotional valence, relate to meaningfulness via distinct patterns of intrinsic need satisfaction. Results from a preregistered, intensive-longitudinal study (144 persons; 6,920 situations) reveal that biographic resonance relates to both high- and low-effort modes of eudaimonic entertainment. Moreover, by linking users’ self-reports with their tracked digital music use (2,786 sessions; 107,147 songs), we find that the occurrence and quality of biographic resonance vary across situations and are shaped by both content and contextual factors within algorithmically curated environments. Our results highlight how resonances between media users’ selves and entertainment content foster situational meaningfulness in everyday life.

Unwelcome shores: Black refugees in America
More than a partisan pandemic: Worldview and COVID ‐19 response in the United States
authors: Marc J. Hetherington, Andrew M. Engelhardt, Isaac D. Mehlhaff
abstract: As the COVID‐19 pandemic unfolded, public responses increasingly divided along political lines: Democrats tended to support policies and behaviors recommended by public health experts and Republicans tended to oppose them. We argue that exclusively party‐based explanations for these patterns are incomplete. Instead, we call attention to people's philosophy about life—their “worldview”—as an important force behind their pandemic responses. We posit that citizens use beliefs derived from interactions with their everyday life to inform their affinities and preferences when analogous matters enter the political realm. Using original cross‐sectional and panel survey data gathered over the course of the pandemic, we theorize and empirically validate a multidimensional measure of worldview. We show that worldview is a coherent, belief‐system‐like entity that remained stable during the pandemic, suggesting its centrality in mass responses to uncertain and novel stimuli. We then show that even before strong party cues emerged, worldview structured Americans' reactions to COVID‐19 and constrained the positions parties could take. Worldview's influence was both direct and indirect, channeled through its relationship with partisan preference. While partisanship is a potent force in political belief systems, much of its effect, we suggest, comes from its association with people's general philosophy about life.

title: Beyond prejudice reduction: Personal and civic effects of intergroup contact among marginalized youth in Northern Ireland
authors: Danielle L. Blaylock, Patrick F. Kotzur, Alexander W. O'Donnell, Rhiannon N. Turner, Stephanie Burns, Laura K. Taylor, Linda R. Tropp
abstract: Intergroup contact reduces prejudice, but its potential to foster broader personal and societal change remains understudied. We address these gaps by examining a large‐scale peacebuilding intervention (PEACE4Youth) among marginalized youth in post‐conflict Northern Ireland. Using latent growth curve modeling across three waves, we demonstrate that increased intergroup contact is associated with improvements not only in youth's outgroup attitudes but also in their self‐esteem, leadership skills, and civic engagement. Youth with steeper contact gains showed the strongest growth across all domains, supporting intergroup contact as a mechanism for multidimensional change. While effects emerged across Catholic and Protestant youth, baseline differences underscore the role of pre‐existing disparities. These findings extend contact theory by empirically linking contact to personal and societal development, redefining it as a tool not only for harmony but also for empowering individuals to transform divided societies.

title: Measuring affective polarization: Matching concepts to measures
authors: James N. Druckman, Samara Klar, Yanna Krupnikov, Matthew Levendusky, John Barry Ryan
abstract: Affective polarization is the extent to which partisans like their own party relative to their dislike of opposing parties. High levels of affective polarization in the United States and many other countries have prompted widespread scholarly interest and practical concern. Yet, despite nearly 15 years of scholarship, significant uncertainty remains about how best to measure affective polarization. We offer a comprehensive review focused on the measurement of affective polarization, underscoring how seemingly innocuous choices can yield substantially different results. These include the target of evaluation (e.g., engaged ideologues, ordinary voters), the dimensions of evaluation (e.g., liking/disliking, moralization), the measurement context (e.g., whether respondents are interviewed by an interviewer or complete surveys independently) and the political context (e.g., the power relationship between parties). We conclude that the next generation of inquiry will need to more carefully align measures of affective polarization with specific research questions.

title: Corporate Quasi‐Sovereignty: Big Tech and the Politics of Sovereign Authority in the Digital Age
authors: Chee Hae Chung, Bryce J. Dietrich
abstract: As private technology firms expand their control over critical infrastructures, questions of sovereignty and governance are increasingly displaced from states to corporate actors. Existing scholarship on sovereignty assumes that authority is either monopolized by states or shared through institutionalized public–private arrangements. Yet, recent events, including SpaceX's control of wartime communications in Ukraine, Meta's confrontation with the Australian government, and OpenAI's attempts to shape global AI regulation, demonstrate that firms can exercise discretionary authority without formal delegation, legal accountability, or democratic oversight. This study introduces the concept of Corporate Quasi‐Sovereignty (CQS) to theorize how certain technology firms function as de facto sovereign actors. CQS is defined by the convergence of three enabling dimensions: infrastructural command, executive autonomy, and normative or geopolitical assertion. Drawing on Kingdon's Multiple Streams Framework (MSF), this paper theorizes ‘sovereignty windows’ as the mechanism through which firms internally collapse the problem, policy, and politics streams, enabling unilateral interventions with geopolitical consequences. ‘Stream collapse,’ the internalization of all three MSF streams within a single corporate hierarchy, is operationalized as a boundary condition of MSF, distinct from conventional stream coupling. The ‘conditional policy entrepreneur’ is introduced as the corporate analogue to Kingdon's entrepreneur: a founder‐CEO who exercises this role only when all three CQS enabling conditions simultaneously converge. Drawing on comparative case analyses of Meta, SpaceX, and OpenAI, the article shows how CQS captures both reactive and anticipatory modes of corporate authority, showing that firms now operate as both market actors and quasi‐sovereign agents capable of substituting, bypassing, or preempting state power.

title: Beyond the ideal type: Investigating ‘mixed preferences’ for who should govern in nine European countries
authors: Sebastien Rojon, Jean-Benoit Pilet, Paulina Pankowska, Davide Vittori, Emilien Paulis
abstract: Noting widespread disenchantment with representative actors and institutions, a growing field of research has investigated public support for decision-making by alternative actors, such as ordinary citizens and independent experts. However, previous research has mainly focused on ideal-type models of government centred on a single actor, rather than considering that citizens may hold ‘mixed preferences’ for multiple actors. Through a latent profile analysis of survey responses to an established battery measuring preferences for who should govern, we identify six preference types that exist across nine European countries, though their prevalence varies from country to country. The results show that only a small minority of respondents support an ideal-type model, i.e., the representative democrats, while most favour a combination of actors. A sizeable share of respondents continues to support politicians but would like to see greater involvement from either citizens or experts. Finally, we identify three profiles that lack strong theoretical or empirical grounding in previous research but emerge across multiple countries and therefore merit further attention: stealth populists, responsible democrats, and moderates.

title: Threat perception and partisan animosity: Evidence from Argentina and Brazil
authors: Raul Gomez, Jose Javier Olivas Osuna, Luis Ramiro
abstract: This study examines antagonism between opposing political camps in Argentina and Brazil, two Latin American countries that have experienced heightened polarization and growing support for contentious right-wing populist leaders. Using original survey data, we analyze how specific perceived threats relate to social distance toward supporters of rival presidential candidates, which we use as a proxy for outgroup animosity. We examine multiple threat domains, including perceived threats from rival political camps, other social groups (racists and immigrants) and threats to symbolic values (equality and the nation). Our findings show that threat perception is a significant correlate of outgroup distance in both countries, but the forms of perceived threat linked to outgroup distancing differ across political camps. We also find partial support for the hypothesis that threat perception is more strongly associated with outgroup distance among supporters of the populist right, particularly once potential confounders are taken into account. While this pattern is evident in Brazil, in Argentina, the left and right camps do not differ significantly in how strongly threat perception predicts outgroup distance.

title: Constructing representation: Political actors’ representative style on Facebook during European and national election campaigns
authors: Márton Bene, Gábor Illés, Uta Russmann, Paweł Baranowski, Jörg Haßler, Simon Kruschinski, Linda Bos, Jakob Linaa Jensen, Anders Olof Larsson, Alena Macková, Anamaria Dutceac Segesten
abstract: This study investigates contemporary forms of political representation by analyzing the Facebook communication of 110 political leaders from eight European countries during both national and 2024 European Parliament (EP) election campaigns. Based on constructivist theories of representation, we introduce the concept of ‘representational style’, defined as the specific combination of six communicative elements: policy focus, personalized communication, direct voter connection, appeals to social groups, references to a homogeneous people, and antagonism toward opponents. Using manual content analysis of 7,854 posts, the study identifies three distinct representational styles through inductive cluster analysis: People’s Policy Warriors, Technocratic-Pluralist Heroes, and (Wo)man of the People. The findings reveal substantial variation across political and national contexts. A clear East–West divide emerges with Western European leaders tending to adopt a Technocratic-Pluralist approach, while Central and Eastern European politicians more often represent themselves as responsive figures closely connected to the people.

title: Intersectionality and the Internet: Race, Class, Gender, Sexuality, and the Digital
authors: Safiya U. Noble, André Brock, Kishonna Gray, Sarah T. Roberts
abstract: Over the past 20 years, the broad field of digital media and technology studies has been influenced by theories of power that include intersectionality as a key organizing theory and method. In this article, we review the major contributions across multiple fields of study, particularly critical race and digital studies, to the examinations of the Internet and technology that use intersectionality as an organizing logic. Applying intersectionality as a conceptual lens into digital technology design, dissemination, and use has aided in findings that the computing industries are ill-equipped to map the world, its conditions, or its inhabitants. In reframing this sociocultural complexity as solvable by mathematics, statistics, code, and data, these industries make dehumanizing political and ethical decisions through reduction—from people and culture to content and abstracting the world to data. In the process, they intentionally reify long-standing inequities in the name of efficiency, progress, and profit and fail to capture what is necessary to improve life in socially, politically, and environmentally just ways. While intersectionality theory is complex, its intricacies afford critical culture digital scholars the epistemological tools and methodological insights needed to highlight that people, communities, and the environment must be considered prior to, in the midst of, and downstream of technoculture's mechanistic, rationalist, extractive desires or capitalism's desires for profit through exploitation.

title: Colorism as a Fundamental Cause of Inequalities in Health
abstract: One of the most influential theories guiding research on the social determinants of health is the theory that socioeconomic status (SES) is a fundamental cause of health inequalities. Nevertheless, the authors of that theory agree that SES is not the only fundamental cause of health worth considering. They, along with other researchers, have identified racism as another important fundamental cause of health inequalities that affects health: ( a ) through its link to SES; ( b ) through its association with flexible resources such as prestige (or status), freedom, and beneficial social connections; and, crucially, ( c ) how it affects multiple disease outcomes through multiple mechanisms above and beyond SES. We argue that colorism, which is a system of discrimination based on the lightness or darkness of one's skin color that is often obscured by or even conflated with racism, is also a fundamental cause of health inequalities for many of the same reasons that racism is. While there is still much to learn about colorism and health, as we acknowledge, there is still enough existing evidence to reasonably conclude that colorism, too, is a fundamental cause of health inequalities—and one that affects health above and beyond both SES and race/ethnicity.

title: When Does Term Length Matter? Party Status, Polarization, and Legislative Productivity
abstract: Longer terms should increase legislative productivity by extending time horizons, yet the empirical evidence for this outcome is inconsistent. This manuscript argues that the effects of term length depend on both party status and polarization. Using data from across U.S. state legislatures, the results demonstrate that the productivity advantages of longer terms depend on the political context. As polarization increases within states over time, the relative benefit of longer terms shifts from minority to majority party members. At low polarization levels, minorities would benefit more from term extensions than majorities. At high polarization, this pattern reverses. These findings reconcile prior research and reveal how the political context can shape institutional effects.

title: Controlling for Oversight in Studies of Oversight
authors: Jenn S. Kim, Benjamin Kinnard, John Patty
abstract: In honor of the creation of the Congressional Oversight Research Database (CORD), we explore some of the selection effects that observable measures of oversight may be subject to. We present a model in which Congress endogenously chooses whether to hold a hearing or to preempt the need for one by overturning an agency's policy in advance. These endogenous oversight choices imply that observable outcomes arise through two pathways: Congress may overturn a policy immediately or only after acquiring additional information through a hearing. Failing to account for this information‐gathering stage can obscure the underlying mechanisms that drive these outcomes. Using data from ProQuest and CORD, we test two implications of the model, finding evidence that Congress selects into conducting oversight hearings and implementing subsequent policy reversals more often when in opposition to the President, with no impact of the information gathered during a hearing on subsequent policy reversals. This implies that Congress uses committee hearings primarily as a mechanism for sharing information about the executive branch when it is politically convenient, rather than as a mechanism for gathering information on policy alternatives. We then conclude with broader implications for empirical research on oversight, including the importance of distinguishing between information gathering and information sharing in oversight.

title: Learning in Committee? How Racial Diversity Shapes Speech, Evidence Use, and Substantive Representation in Congress
abstract: Research on descriptive representation has primarily examined whether and how descriptive representatives themselves advance group interests. In the context of race, this work shows that nonwhite lawmakers advance nonwhite interests, but less is known about whether nonwhite representation also shapes white lawmakers' behavior. I argue that repeated contact with nonwhite lawmakers in racially diverse committees may shape how white Democrats engage race‐related issues, making them more likely to support race‐related hearing statements with evidence. To test this expectation, I combine large‐scale text classification with a detailed content analysis of more than 11,000 race‐related committee hearing statements and 87,000 full bill texts from the 105th–117th Congresses. Using a within‐legislator design, I find that white Democrats serving on racially diverse committees are more likely to cite evidence when discussing race and to cite the same sources as their nonwhite colleagues. I also show that race‐based expertise is associated with substantive representation: legislators who more frequently cite evidence when discussing race are more effective at advancing race‐related legislation. Together, these findings suggest that descriptive representation may foster substantive representation, in part, by shaping how white Democrats engage race‐related issues in racially diverse legislative committees.

title: “We are not criminals!” Stuckness and existential tactics among residents at a Danish deportation center
authors: Martin Lindhardt, Freja Lindberg Birkelund, Annika Vistisen Lidegaard
abstract: Based on qualitative research in a Danish deportation center, Kærshovedgaard, this article explores residents’ experiences of stuckness while also shedding light on their existential struggles to transform the world into which they were thrown into a world they had a hand in making. In pursuing an analysis of stuckness as a multifaceted experience comprising temporal, spatial, legal, and categorical dimensions, we engage with scholarly literature on liminality and waiting. We further draw on the existential anthropology of Michael Jackson, coupled with Michel de Certeau’s concept of tactical agency in our exploration of how residents, while being faced with overwhelming circumstances, struggled to salvage some semblance of comprehension and control in governing their own lives. We show how the agency of residents was in large part related to negotiations of social positions and statuses other than detainee, or of not being reduced to ascribed identities.

title: Suspended solidarity: the experience of precarity and the chronopolitics of support in Australia’s asylum regime
abstract: This article examines how the Australian asylum regime’s chronopolitics, the strategic use of indefinite delays, actively constructs a state of indeterminate liminality for both people seeking asylum and the associated support sector. Drawing on ethnographic data, it is argued that bureaucratic processes function as systems of suffering, where weaponized time serves as a tool of affective violence. The support sector faces a fundamental chronopolitical tension as it navigates a punitive state apparatus. The system’s design co-opts supporters’ sustained commitments, to be consumed by the protracted limbo of the asylum process. This shared temporal condition is characterized by an exhaustion of potentiality, where state-sanctioned stalling prevents those seeking refuge from constructing meaningful futures while simultaneously consuming the agency of the supporter in a cycle of permanent crisis management. The regime’s designed precarity perpetuates this bureaucratic stasis, resulting in suspended solidarity and constituting an embedded form of bureaucratic violence.
