Legislative Pork‐Barrel Funding and Public Policy Outcomes: The Role of Local‐Level Factors
abstract: The growing legislative influence over budget allocations through pork‐barrel funding raises concerns that this type of distributive policy may undermine effectiveness. We examine Brazil's mandatory pork‐barrel system to assess whether funding availability affects health outcomes and how local conditions shape these effects. We focus on municipalities' abilities to attract resources (“funding concentration”) and their autonomy over investment decisions (“funding flexibility”), with expectations conditioned by administrative capacity. Using panel data on 4114 Brazilian municipalities (2015–2021) and controlling for endogeneity and selection bias, we find that pork‐barrel funding is associated with higher short‐term rates of preventable hospitalizations. These effects dissipate over time but reveal how political‐electoral dynamics shape implementation. Such dynamics undermine the expected benefits of administrative capacity, suggesting that political oversight patterns condition policy outcomes. Evidence on funding concentration indicates that, in contexts of politically allocated funding, administrative capacity may facilitate the rapid execution of concentrated, electoral‐driven allocations, which can amplify inefficiencies. These findings highlight the importance of aligning legislative budget governance with local administrative capacity to mitigate the risks of funding fragmentation and ensure more effective governance of distributive policies.

How to Upend America in 100 Days: Unilateral Power at the Outset of Trump’s Second Term
abstract: President Trump used the unilateral power of the presidency in extraordinary ways during the first 100 days of his second term. This article examines his use of executive action using a dataset of every action issued in the first 100 days of Trump’s second term, along with a similar dataset for his first term and other recent administrations. At the outset of his second term, Trump issued substantially more executive actions than his own first administration and his recent predecessors; however, this also came with historically low legislative productivity. His unilateral policy making is notable for the many revocations of previous executive actions and startling uses of the pardon power. The areas that Trump acted within most were government operations, tariff policies, and policies related to law and crime. These findings reveal important details of Trump’s unilateral presidency and demonstrate that his executive actions are likely to erode the traditional boundaries of presidency power if not held in check by other institutional actors.

title: Predatory Journals: Do They Publish Undergraduate and AI-Generated Papers?
abstract: Predatory journals are criticized widely for weak peer-review and profit-driven editorial practices, but little empirical evidence assesses their capacity to publish low-quality or AI-generated research. This study examines the level to which these journals publish undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts. We submitted papers to 144 predatory journals identified through spam solicitations, Beall’s list ( https://beallslist.net ), and the Predatory Journals database ( www.predatoryjournals.org/news/predatory-journals-list-2025 ). This included 19 undergraduate political science and human rights essays and 10 AI-generated engineering case reports to test the degree to which these essays are published. We find that most undergraduate essays and AI-generated manuscripts are accepted, which confirms the low quality of these outlets and the risk emanating from them.

title: Beyond the Greenback: Currency Power in a Greener, More Fragmented World
abstract: Structural shifts in the global economy are reshaping the foundations of international currency power. This article explores how the green transition, geopolitical realignment, and sustained US protectionism could interact to transform the global currency hierarchy, with a particular focus on the US dollar and the Chinese renminbi (RMB). We highlight two key drivers of currency usage: (1) the liquidity and availability of a currency for cross-border transactions; and (2) the strategic economic and political alignment between currency issuers and their partners. Considering developments in green value chains, evolving alliances, and trade policies, the article outlines how China’s growing role in critical minerals, infrastructure finance, and alternative financial systems can enhance the internationalization of the RMB. Concurrently, US protectionism and withdrawal from multilateralism may open up space for regional currency diversification. These trends point to an increasingly fragmented and multipolar international monetary system, in which currency power will have a central role in shaping the future global order.

title: Institutionalized Enforcement of Administrative Compliance: State Regulator Use of Noncompliance Burdens
abstract: Administrative burden scholarship typically examines rules and regulations affecting access to public benefits during initial citizen-state interactions. Scholars agree that individual burdens function as “hidden politics” because policy changes during implementation through bureaucratic discretion. Less is known about bureaucratic behavior or hidden politics enforced on third-party service providers maintaining compliance. In this article we address this by examining noncompliance burdens imposed on abortion providers to understand if regulators emulate peers’ behavior. Using an institutional theoretical framework and administrative records from the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration (FAHCA) on abortion provider oversight, we construct a directed dyadic event history model using 1540 dyad-year observations to predict isomorphism or divergence of sanction activities across regulatory field offices. We find that regulatory field offices emulate behavior of others based on peer’s previous sanction behavior and oversight workload. We also find that regulators diverge from peers based on the regulatory conditions of their own jurisdiction.

Infelicitous Political Talk: Disparaging Institutions and Support for Democracy
authors: James L. Gibson, Michael J. Nelson
abstract: Infelicitous political talk is now a routine feature of American politics, with scholars debating the extent to which it meaningfully shapes citizens’ democratic attitudes. We seek to contribute to this body of work by showing that the degree of inappropriateness of a criticism is continuous and subjective; that rhetorical denigration of democratic institutions is more likely to influence evaluations of the speaker than to erode broader commitments to democracy; and that criticisms that “cross the line” of appropriateness can create backlashes that actually wind up increasing support for democratic institutions and values. Using an experiment embedded in a national survey, we evaluate the effects of inappropriate attacks on the U.S. judiciary. Perceived rhetorical denigration does not weaken democratic values; instead, it produces a small but consistent backlash that slightly increases support for democratic institutions. Our various findings strongly challenge the assumption that rising infelicitous talk poses a serious threat to democratic stability in the U.S.

When the party is over: How parties respond to electoral decline
abstract: Over the past decades, we have witnessed the severe electoral decline of formerly successful parties. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how these parties have responded to their losses. I examine the consequences of severe and persistent electoral losses through the lens of intra-party dynamics. I argue that parties react to severe decline by shifting attention to core issues and adopting more extreme positions. I theorize that this is because office-seekers are the first to abandon the sinking ship, tilting the internal power balance towards policy-motivated actors. Testing the theory with manifesto data from 18 Western European countries between 1970 and 2025, I find evidence that parties devote more attention to their core issues following their electoral decline. Parties do not, however, adopt more extreme positions on these issues. I find limited evidence that shifts in the intra-party balance are behind these changes.

title: Allocative claims and pork barrel politics
authors: Marius Sältzer, Hauke Peters, Charlotte Keyßler
abstract: Political strategies are shaped by electoral institutions and incentives. There is a large literature on pork barrel politics in single-member districts (SMD), but understanding the institutional effects that shape the incentives for pork requires comparison within the same system. The German Mixed-Member Electoral system offers an ideal institutional setup, but official data on pork is not available. Instead, we focus on the use of pork references as an electoral strategy, adapting credit-claiming theory to textual analysis of candidates’ social media posts. Using supervised machine learning on Facebook posts by candidates in the 2017 and 2021 federal election campaign period, we fine-tune a BERT classifier on 1000 manually coded posts to identify pork references (F1: 0.82). Our results demonstrate that incumbents, particularly district incumbents and those who outperform their national party’s vote share, are significantly more likely to emphasize pork in their communication. Moreover, candidates are more likely to use pork references if their competitors within the district employ similar strategies, and when electoral competition in the district is high. Our findings imply that particularistic logic exists beyond SMDs and can be shaped by the internal specificities of more complex incentive systems.

title: Party responsiveness to party supporters, the electorate, and interest groups in a multidimensional policy space
abstract: This article sheds new light on party responsiveness by considering the role of interest group pressure in parties’ responsiveness to their supporters and the electorate on multiple policy dimensions in 12 countries. Following recent work, we expect that parties are as responsive to shifts in their supporters’ preferences as to the wider electorate. Yet, parties also attend to interest group pressure. We argue that parties’ responsiveness to voters is enhanced by leadership ties with interest groups but that ties with only sectional groups are associated with more stable party positions. Combining data on voters, interest groups, and parties, our analysis shows that parties are responsive to preference change among their supporters and, further, that their policy positions are more stable when they only have ties with sectional groups. However, parties’ responsiveness on specific dimensions is not necessarily enhanced by leadership ties with the interest groups particularly active on those dimensions.

title: Technocracy or not, this is the question: can party system predict the number of technocrats in governments?
abstract: In the last three decades, Europe has witnessed an increase in the number of technocrats – non-partisan, non-elected experts appointed on the basis of technical competence – in government. This paper examines whether structural characteristics of party systems predict the share of technocrats in cabinets across 30 European countries between 2000 and 2024. Building on theories of party competition, delegation, and representation, it investigates how systemic features of party democracy shape technocratic appointments. Using fractional regression models, the study tests the relationship between the share of technocrats and three key party-system variables: ideological polarization, party system fragmentation, and party institutionalization. The findings reveal that technocrats are significantly more prevalent where ideological distance between parties complicates bargaining and creates demand for neutral mediators who can bridge incompatible policy positions. Conversely, when more parties compete for portfolios, partisan actors crowd out non-partisan experts rather than delegating to them. Most importantly, in systems where parties possess stable organizations, coherent programmatic profiles, and deep societal roots, technocratic inclusion is significantly lower.

A dynamic seat product model
abstract: The Seat Product Model uses just two institutional parameters (average district magnitude and assembly size) to predict legislative fragmentation with remarkable accuracy. However, it is best suited for simple, single-tier systems. Subsequent extensions to complex, two-tier systems rely on an upper-tier (multiplier-style) correction that accounts for cross-tier inflationary effects but estimate it as a single constant from pooled cross-national data. Applied to Mexico’s mixed-member lower house elections (1997–2021), both specifications systematically mispredict legislative fragmentation. This is because cross-tier inflationary effects are not a fixed system property but an evolving one, shaped by institutional features interacting with a changing party system. This study proposes a Dynamic Seat Product Model that retains the original institutional baseline while allowing the correction to update automatically via exponential smoothing. The DSPM tracks Mexico’s long-run rise in legislative fragmentation more closely than fixed alternatives, clarifies the mechanism behind it, and offers a principled path toward making the SPM applicable to virtually any single election.

Estimation and inference for the persistence of extremely high temperatures
authors: Juan-Juan Cai, Yicong Lin, Julia Schaumburg, Chenhui Wang
abstract: We propose a nonparametric framework for estimating the extremal index that captures the persistence of extreme observations. The framework provides unified and simple procedures for verifying the well-known local dependence condition D(d)(un), which characterizes the extremal index yet is often assessed through heuristic checks, and for selecting d (a key parameter for estimation) when the condition holds. Under a general φ-mixing condition, we establish the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator and prove the consistency of both the tuning parameter selection and the verification procedure for the D(d)(un) condition. Simulation studies show improved performance relative to two commonly used methods in terms of empirical mean squared errors. We analyze summer apparent temperature data for nine European cities from 1940 to 2025. The results show strong evidence of persistence in extreme temperatures for all cities, with such extremes typically lasting at least two days. The probability of two-day extreme-temperature events is two to four times higher in the most recent three decades relative to 1940–1974.

title: Does populism challenge the status quo? Understanding transgression and subversion in contemporary politics
abstract: This article argues that we need to distinguish between transgression and subversion in order to fully understand populism and contemporary politics more generally. We make three key contributions. First, we revisit contemporary scholarship on transgression, arguing that existing distinctions between different forms of norm-breaking do not fully explain their markedly different political effects. Second, drawing on psychoanalysis, particularly the concepts of fantasy and enjoyment, we foreground the role of affective and libidinal investment in shaping political identification. From this perspective, transgression may reaffirm the socio-normative order rather than challenge it. Third, we introduce the concept of subversion to offer greater analytical granularity when studying political movements and parties that challenge the status quo. While transgression may revitalise the norm through the enjoyment generated by its violation, subversion loosens the affective attachments through which socio-normative arrangements acquire their grip. By disentangling transgression from subversion, we call for a more fine-grained understanding of populist politics and advocate a rethinking of what subversive politics means today.

title: Cyclicality in reactionary internationalism: A genealogy of Realist, Spenglerian, and New Right theories of historical change
abstract: Reactionary actors from Lavrov to Trump often appeal to ‘realism’ in denouncing the liberal rights-based international order. What makes Realism and contemporary New Right ethno-nationalist politics conceptually compatible? Examining the intertwined intellectual histories of their conceptualisations of time and historical change, we find that early Realism adopted from ethno-geopolitics a theory of historical change as perpetually recurring cycles of survivalist struggle. We first retrieve the intellectual history of cyclical theories in international thought and Realist traditions, showing how they were drawn from 19th-century German ethno-geopolitics. Second, we map their influence on contemporary New Right nationalism. The history of cyclical temporal theory reveals that early Realism and ethno-nationalism emerged as related and compatible strategies to manage Western decline. While most Realist International Relations isn’t necessarily ethno-nationalist, its theorisation of historical change as cyclical rise and decline through survivalist struggle has nonetheless come to support the global resurgence of New Right ethno-nationalism.

title: Presumed media influence and support for social media bans: The roles of social and elite-based validation
authors: Sarah Geber, Anne Schulz, Mike S. Schäfer, Thomas N. Friemel
abstract: The study examines how presumed influences of social media on young people, as well as perceptions of how widely such beliefs are shared, shape support for social media bans. Extending the Influence of Presumed Influence (IPI) model, we introduce second-order presumed influences, defined as perceptions about how widely others presume media influences, and propose a mechanism of social validation. We additionally examine elite-based validation, referring to perceived beliefs of influential actors (i.e. scientists, politicians, and the media), as well as perceived social norms. Using survey data ( N = 1270) collected in the context of debates about a social media ban for minors under 16 in Switzerland, we find that stronger presumed influences predict support for a ban. While we find no support for social validation, the results point to the relevance of elite-related perceptions, particularly presumed scientific consensus. Perceived social norms of ban support emerge as an additional predictor of regulatory preferences.

title: Rethinking platform vernaculars: Collective practices and power dynamics in platform environments
abstract: In 2015, Gibbs et al. introduced the concept of platform vernaculars to describe how communicative genres emerge through interactions between platform affordances and user practices. Although widely adopted in media research, the concept has not been systematically refined in light of recent developments in affordance theory and platform studies. Drawing on an integrative literature review, this paper revisits platform vernaculars as plural, recognizable, repeatable, temporarily stabilized, and contested formations emerging through collective negotiations of affordances within platform environments. The paper further introduces four heuristic categories–intended vernaculars, dominant vernaculars, community vernaculars, and counter-public vernaculars–to discuss how communicative norms, genres, and modes of participation become normalized, marginalized, contested, or transformed across platforms. By rethinking platform vernaculars, the paper offers a systematic analytical framework for studying platform practices and norms. Furthermore, it positions vernaculars as a lens for analyzing platform power and user agency, opening avenues for future research.

title: Do elite cues affect public opinion? Evidence from Switzerland's EU negotiation breakdown
abstract: On 26 May 2021, the Swiss Federal Council announced the unilateral termination of negotiations with the European Union on the institutional framework agreement, effectively abandoning a years-long effort to formalize bilateral relations. We study if this decision functioned as an elite cue about Switzerland's future relationship with the European Union, influencing public attitudes toward European integration. Using survey data from May to June 2021, we employ a regression discontinuity design leveraging interview timing around the announcement. Our findings suggest the announcement prompted a modest shift in public opinion, with some evidence from ordinary least squares models indicating a stronger response among French-speaking respondents. We discuss the implications for studying elite cues in direct-democratic contexts, suggesting that salient political events may generate limited change even when signals are ambiguous and the political context makes such effects rather unlikely.

title: Bridging global ambition and local reality: African insights for the future of the Belém Adaptation Indicators
Regions, welfare state services, and the political economy of growth regimes
authors: Emmanuele Pavolini, Luigi Burroni, Dario Raspanti, Enzo Valentini
abstract: This essay advances an understanding of the extent to which political economies have changed in the ‘era of knowledge-based growth’. It emphasizes the importance of considering not only the country level but also the sub-national regional level of socio-economic dynamics, as well as the role of welfare state services. This contribution provides three main findings based on an ad-hoc dataset built by collecting different types of socio-economic information at the regional level. First, it demonstrates how the welfare state is playing an increasingly pivotal role as a direct ‘growth engine’. Second, it shows the emergence of complex and diversified economic specialization and growth models at the sub-national level. Third, two major types of political economies are identified that are characterized by differing degrees of territorial integration of their regional economic specialization and growth models. The identified ‘typology’ of national political economies only partially overlaps with the most common ones described in comparative political economy literature.

title: Adaptive network responses to financial shocks: evidence from Bitcoin transaction data
authors: Marco Venturini, Daniel García-Costa, Flaminio Squazzoni
abstract: Bitcoin has evolved from being an alternative to becoming part of the global financial market, boasting 800 million users and institutional investors. This raises the question of whether digital assets and traditional financial markets exhibit similar dynamics, particularly during periods of uncertainty and global shocks. Bitcoin’s data is ideal for studying the effect of information shocks on micro-financial structures and informing current socio-economic research on network finance and uncertainty. To study how the structure of the Bitcoin transaction network evolves during periods of uncertainty, we examined 137 million transactions before and after the two most significant Bitcoin shocks: the 2014 Mt. Gox crisis and the 2020 pandemic. We focused on detecting network patterns that reveal uncertainty reduction mechanisms: inertia, trust, generalised exchange, and referral. Different adaptive patterns emerged: during the Mt. Gox crisis, the network changed long-term patterns while maintaining short-term stability; during the 2020 pandemic, however, the network adapted in the short term while maintaining long-term stability. We suggest that this adaptive asymmetry reflects institutional investors transmitting shocks in the short-term across parts of the global financial market while increasing Bitcoin stability. Our findings confirm that Bitcoin is now a systemically relevant part of the global financial market, raising the question of its institutional regulation.

title: Outsider orbit: segmentation of employment trajectories and feminisation of outsiders in South Korea
abstract: This article examines the segmentation of the South Korean labour market based on workers’ employment trajectory patterns. Over the decades, labour market segmentation literature has explained labour market inequality by investigating non-competing segments that advantage certain workers over others–namely, insiders over outsiders. Nevertheless, despite increasingly diverse employment trajectories in post-industrialised societies, little is known about how the labour market is segmented when considering job mobility over time. Against this background, this article uses group-based multi-trajectory modelling on Korean Labor & Income Panel Study data to investigate labour market segmentation patterns based on long-term employment trajectories. Our findings reveal clear evidence of a segmented labour market, with three types of outsiders exhibiting distinct employment trajectories compared to two types of insiders, and married women being over-represented across all outsider trajectories. We argue that outsiders are trapped in ‘outsider orbits’, a structural barrier that limits women to outsider status in Korea.

title: Marriage as a resource: family marriage strategies among elites in response to institutional change
authors: Niccolò Giorgio Armandola, Malte Doehne, Katja Rost
abstract: Marital sorting is commonly used by elites to prevent status erosion and maintain exclusivity. However, elites are affected by shifts in the socioeconomic environment, and their capacity to navigate such challenges determines their long-term success. We use genealogical data from early modern Switzerland to analyze 14,841 marriages in Basel between 1648 and 1848, a period marked by legislative reform, to examine how elites adjusted their marriage strategies to institutional change and how these adjustments affected family social status. Switzerland offers a compelling setting for studying elites because of its high wealth concentration and the importance of old elite dynasties. Our findings show that Basel’s old elite adopted conservative, endogamous strategies as reforms threatened their political privileges, even as an emergent silk merchant elite continued selective exogamy into the old elite. More broadly, the effectiveness of family marriage strategies was shaped by the institutional rules governing families' access to power.

title: Techno-Climentality: Digital Technologies and the Transformation of Environmental Governance (SI)
abstract: Climate technologies, “nature tech,” and digital earth infrastructures are now rapidly proliferating as tools to monitor and manage changing environments. Such technologies remake the actors, sites, institutions, and practices involved in environmental governance. They can transplant governance from state to nonstate actors and from public to private institutions. They can also forestall more full-scale social, political, and ecological change needed to address the root causes of climate change. Building on the concept of “cli-mentality” from Steig and Oels (2025), this research article proposes a technology-centric investigation in the form of “techno-climentality” to analyze the consequences of these proliferating devices and infrastructures. Through interview, survey, and case study research on digitalizing forests in locations worldwide, we show how technology-led environmental governance can create unequal power, resource, and knowledge practices, along with transformations in community engagement. Techno-climentality centers on how digital technologies can depoliticize and remove environmental governance from wider accountability, yet also be transformed toward more pluralistic and just practices of governance.

title: Repression as Aesthetic Ordering: How UK Universities Make Palestine Solidarity Illegible in a Time of Genocide
abstract: This paper analyzes the repression of Palestine solidarity activism on UK university campuses following October 7, 2023. To explain why institutions whose mission centers on critical inquiry and open debate have enacted far-reaching restrictions on Palestine solidarity, we compile an original dataset of 114 incidents across 70 universities (October 2023–March 2025). Drawing on Jacques Rancière’s concept of the “distribution of the sensible,” we conceptualize repression not simply as deterrence or punishment but as a mode of aesthetic ordering through which universities govern political visibility and legitimacy. Repression is multilayered, operating through coercive enforcement and legal actions, procedural and bureaucratic controls, punitive disciplinary processes, and the symbolic erasure of visual and affective expressions of dissent. These practices are enabled by—and in turn reinforce—neoliberal managerialism, racialized securitization, and imperial governance logics that produce racialized hierarchies of threat and safety and recode solidarity as risk and disruption. By rendering Palestine solidarity illegible and illegitimate as politics, UK universities contribute to conditions through which genocidal violence becomes tolerable.

title: The Lock-In Effect and the Corporate Payout Puzzle,
abstract: Taxes on capital gains are deferred until realization whereas dividends are taxed upon accrual. This often makes dividends tax disadvantaged relative to share repurchases, which leads to the payout puzzle: why do firms pay dividends? This paper demonstrates that tax deferment can also provide a solution to this puzzle: if shareholders with an accrued capital gain and a non-zero investment horizon demand a premium to sell equity—as compensation for accelerated realizations (and taxation)—then dividends can become tax efficient. This mechanism is appealing because it can explain dividend payments without appealing to asymmetric information, incomplete contracting, repurchase constraints, and/or irrationality.

title: Shifting Sands: Past, Present, and Future of Coastal Dunes
authors: M. Luisa Martínez, Patrick A. Hesp, Rodolfo Silva, Juan B. Gallego-Fernández, Alicia T.R. Acosta, Joana Gaspar de Freitas, Octavio Pérez-Maqueo, Pedro A. Garzo, Karla Salgado, Rusty Feagin, Patricia Moreno-Casasola, Debora Lithgow, Gabriela Mendoza-González, Carmelo Maximiliano-Cordova, Valeria Chávez
abstract: Sandy beaches and coastal dunes are ecologically and culturally valuable environments that support unique biodiversity and provide essential ecosystem services, including recreation, scenic beauty, and storm protection. This review summarizes dune formation processes, global distribution, and plant adaptations to sandy environments (psammophilous vegetation). Coastal dunes are increasingly threatened by direct impacts such as urbanization, mining, and dune stabilization, as well as by indirect pressures from climate change, including sea-level rise, erosion, and vegetation growth driven by warming and changes in precipitation. These combined effects lead to habitat loss, degradation, and the expansion of invasive species. Long-term changes in wave and wind regimes further alter dune dynamics. Assessing dune ecosystems with modern tools, including artificial intelligence, is essential for understanding their current condition and for guiding sustainable management strategies to conserve them.
