Our chapter contributes a more nuanced understanding of how normative functions of state-led ecosystem valuation and environmental interventions in an illiberal context may lead to the overutilization of natural resources that exacerbates stratification and injustice in top-down, centralized environmental governance models.

title: Ethanol Blending in India: Navigating the Dual Crisis of Energy Security and Climate Commitments
abstract: India faces a dual crisis: an oil import dependency of 87.7% costing $137 billion annually, and binding climate commitments including a 47% emission intensity reduction target and net zero by 2070. The transport sector, which accounts for 14% of India's total emissions and 58-60% of imported crude oil consumption, sits at the centre of both crises. This policy brief examines ethanol blending as a policy instrument positioned to address both simultaneously. Drawing on official government data, a peer-reviewed study by IIM-A and the Potsdam Institute (Jha et al., 2026), and the Parliament statement of July 20, 2026, the brief analyses the advantages and challenges of India's Ethanol Blending Programme, which achieved its 20% blending target in 2025, five years ahead of schedule. While the programme has delivered $19.3 billion in forex savings and a net reduction of 832 lakh metric tonnes of CO2 emissions, it presents serious trade-offs in food security, water stress, and land use. This brief argues that the path forward lies not in retreating from ethanol blending, but in accelerating the transition from first-generation sugarcane-based ethanol to second-generation agricultural waste-based ethanol. Five policy recommendations are proposed to address the structural challenges while preserving the programme's strategic benefits.

title: Playing the Spread: The Implications of Worker Volatility for Human Capital Management
abstract: Workers have good days and bad days, but human capital management research overwhelmingly focuses on mean performance. This paper examines whether organizations recognize and price worker volatility when they can measure it, and whether they should. In two studies using data from professional basketball, I document both wage and normative penalties for volatile workers. After separating persistent volatility from playing-time noise, more volatile players earn less on the margin where contracts are negotiable. A difference-in-differences design then exploits the quasi-random timing of absences as an identifying shock. Holding mean performance fixed, losing a reliable player inflicts a larger penalty on team point differential and win probability than losing a volatile one. I show that the steadiest players are nearly as costly to lose as high-mean stars, at forty percent of the salary. Taken together, these results suggest that performance management is a portfolio problem and worker volatility is an important locus for strategic action.

title: Disrupting the Domestic-to-Academic Abuse Relay (DAR): A Framework for Naming and Interrupting the Domestic-to-Academic Handoff of Violence
abstract: This paper introduces Disrupting the Domestic-to-Academic Abuse Relay (DAR), a framework for identifying and interrupting the point at which behavioral and relational patterns learned in domestic environments — including exposure to intimate partner violence (IPV), coercive control, or abusive discipline — are transmitted into school settings as bullying, aggression, or victimization. DAR draws on social learning theory, ecological systems theory, and research on Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) to reframe this transmission using a relay-race metaphor: a series of discrete, observable "handoffs" at which intervention can interrupt the pattern before it advances to the next stage of a person's life. The paper extends DAR into a four-leg lifespan model, the Full Relay, tracing potential transmission from the domestic environment through school, adolescent and early-adult relationships, and adult relational outcomes. It further proposes human-animal co-regulation — grounded in existing human-animal interaction (HAI) research — as an underexamined protective factor, illustrated through a single-subject case observation. DAR is offered as a pedagogical and clinical tool: a vocabulary that makes an abstract risk trajectory visible and teachable to parents, educators, and clinicians.

title: Authoritarian environmentalism and environmental regulation enforcement: A case study of medical waste crime in northwestern China
authors: KuoRay Mao, Yiliang Zhu, Zhong Zhao, Shan Yan
abstract: This chapter offers one of the first studies to examine critically the connection between deficiencies in China’s regulatory apparatus and the criminality associated with illegal dumping and trading of medical waste—specifically as it pertains to waste dumping in rural northwestern China. The authors begin with a brief review of green criminology’s approach to waste crime and summarise the literature on top-down environmental regulation enforcement in China. Next, they describe the development of the medical waste regulation framework and highlight the current obstacles to enforcement in China. The chapter then introduces a case study to illustrate how institutional incentives in the job performance evaluation system of bureaucrats resulted in the under-enforcement of medical waste regulations at the level of rural governance. Their chapter concludes by suggesting that to study environmental offenses in China, green criminologists must examine how the institutional practices of the fragmented bureaucracy shape the economic, political, and social contexts that have structured the complexity of environmental regulation enforcement in this illiberal and restrictive society.

title: At the crossroads of art and science: a typology for epistemic innovation, diversity, and interculturality
abstract: This chapter offers a typology to discover and explore various forms of interaction between art and science. It shows how these interactions operate across three stages of the research cycle: 1) inquiry (the science of art / the art of science), 2) methodology (arts-based research methods / scientific methods to study art), and 3) communication (art communication / communication through art), illustrated through examples. Across these levels, the chapter emphasizes art as an epistemic contribution rather than an instrument. Artistic practices introduce ways of perceiving, understanding, questioning, and critiquing that scientific research alone cannot generate. Art can foster new forms of engagement with scientific content, act as a catalyst for conceptual thinking, and support the translation and communication of complex ideas. Furthermore, artistic approaches can help open scientific inquiry to greater epistemic diversity and intercultural perspectives that remain underrepresented in predominantly Eurocentric research traditions. At the same time, science can inspire new artistic forms, inform artistic translation, and open conceptual space within artistic practice. In this sense, art and science are understood as distinct yet mutually enriching ways of knowing that together generate, translate, and communicate knowledge in new ways, creating opportunities for epistemic innovation at their intersection. The typology provides a framework through which scholars, professionals, and artists can reflect on how art and science intersect and how these intersections contribute to scientific research, artistic practice, and more inclusive and diverse knowledge cultures.

title: The Blueway and the Red Line Spiderweb: Assessing the Impact of Repressive and Ideological State Apparatuses on Environmental Protests in China
authors: KuoRay Mao, Zhong Zhao, Yue Xu
abstract: This study examines China's environmental governance through the framework of Althusser's Repressive and Ideological State Apparatuses, using the 2021 Shenzhen Blueway Ecological Belt Project as a case study. Despite the formalization of public participation, the authoritarian state employs legal, bureaucratic, and ideological mechanisms to suppress dissent while preserving legitimacy. The findings reveal how control over information flows and media narratives, coupled with legal and bureaucratic constraints on NGOs, systematically undermines public engagement and reinforces top-down governance. The Shenzhen case demonstrates the state's dual strategy of repression and ideological control, wherein environmental governance operates both as a political instrument and a means of consolidating state authority. By co-opting NGOs, restricting transparency, and framing environmental contention as a national security threat, the state effectively neutralizes opposition and fortifies its state-capitalist accumulation model. This study contributes to the discourse on authoritarian environmentalism, underscoring its long-term implications for sustainability, public participation, and state-society relations.

title: An External Balance Model for Depopulated Rural Communities: Sensitivity Analysis of Self-Sufficiency Conditions Enabled by AI-Augmented Remote-Income Workers
abstract: Rural policy in Japan has long presupposed population recovery, a premise that no longer holds as the nation enters a phase of demographic contraction. This study inverts the question: under what conditions can a depopulated mountainous community of approximately 500 residents sustain a positive external balance without subsidies? We construct a monthly external-balance model (120 months) that treats the community as a minimal open economy, calibrate living-cost parameters with official statistics (National Medical Expenditure estimates, the Survey of Household Expenditure on Education, and the Family Income and Expenditure Survey), and conduct a 1,875-case sensitivity analysis across three axes: per-capita monthly external income of “remote-income workers” — a portfolio comprising remotely employed staff, licensed professionals, AI- augmented contractors, and content/e-commerce operators — the share of such workers in the population, and fixed infrastructure maintenance costs. The baseline scenario (¥400,000/month per worker, approximately equal to the national average salary of ¥4.78 million/year; a 12% worker share; ¥12 million/month infrastructure cost) achieves subsidy-free surplus, as do 84% of all cases. Our principal finding, however, concerns robustness rather than the surplus rate itself: recalibrating living costs with official statistics left the surplus rate nearly unchanged (86% to 84%), revealing that the conclusion is governed by a single unmeasured variable — hamlet-level infrastructure cost, which no public statistics capture because hamlets are not accounting units of local government. We further show that under adverse conditions no single policy lever restores surplus, whereas simultaneous deployment of four levers reverses the balance (from −¥6.45 million to +¥5.90 million/month) through a dynamic synergy that halts the depopulation spiral. The full model is released as open-source software (MIT license), providing a verifiable common basis for rural policy design that does not presuppose population growth. Note: The full manuscript is written in Japanese; an English abstract is provided above.

title: The Occupational Trauma Compounding Model: Structural Selection and the Deepening of Psychological Harm in the U.S. Service Industry
abstract: The U.S. service industry employs nearly 17 million people and is disproportionately populated by individuals with histories of early adversity, yet no single framework connects the scattered evidence on this workforce across occupational health psychology, trauma psychology, labor economics, and addiction research. This paper advances the Occupational Trauma Compounding Model (OTCM), an integrative theoretical account arguing that the industry structurally selects for trauma-exposed workers and then compounds psychological harm through occupational, physiological, and legal mechanisms, with a distinct symptom picture that persists after workers exit. The model is organized across four levels: (1) structural and psychological selection; (2) occupational entrenchment through trauma bonding, coworker identity fusion, harassment and violence, and the legal exploitation of salaried managers; (3) physiological compounding via substance use, sleep disruption, and nutritional deficiency; and (4) post-industry sequelae that existing diagnostic frameworks systematically misclassify. The paper situates the model against the dominant occupational-stress frameworks — job demands–resources, demand–control, and effort–reward imbalance — and against the burnout construct, arguing that the OTCM adds a selection layer beneath them, an attachment mechanism within them, and a persistence claim beyond them. Synthesizing evidence across published literatures and national datasets, the paper specifies twelve falsifiable propositions and the study designs that would test them, addresses the central identification problem of separating selection from causation, and outlines clinical and policy implications. Primary survey data collection is underway. The OTCM is offered as a testable research agenda for an under-recognized population.

title: Governing AI in Viet Nam: Centralised digital sovereignty and controlled interdependence
abstract: In debates on digital sovereignty, states seek to build the technological and regulatory capacity to govern dependence on foreign digital infrastructures. AI complicates this ambition because its development relies on globally concentrated chips, cloud services, foundation models, capital and technical expertise. This article examines how Viet Nam seeks to build domestic AI capability while remaining integrated into global technology markets. Drawing on qualitative document analysis of Viet Nam’s legal and policy instruments, together with records of foreign AI and infrastructure partnerships, the article conceptualises Viet Nam’s approach as developmental digital sovereignty through controlled interdependence. Viet Nam combines risk-based AI regulation, national AI and data infrastructure, public support for domestic innovation and strategic coordination of technology development with continued foreign investment, research partnerships and technology cooperation. The analysis identifies a non-exclusionary variant of centralised digital sovereignty in which state coordination over infrastructure, data and regulation coexists with continuing foreign participation. It finds stronger evidence of policy aspiration and regulatory access than of material leverage over critical chips, cloud infrastructure or models. However, this strategy remains politically ambiguous. The institutions intended to strengthen domestic compute, data and research capacity also centralise regulatory authority, expand executive discretion and provide limited publicly visible mechanisms for independent oversight. The article argues that developmental digital sovereignty should be assessed through both its capacity to reshape external technological dependence and the accountability conditions governing the domestic exercise of technological power.

title: Changing cropping patterns and vulnerability of small farmers in Marathwada region, India
abstract: Cropping decisions are not always autonomous, but the result of structural factors that govern markets and policies. This article explores the vulnerabilities resulting from cropping pattern changes in the water stressed Marathwada region in India. We draw upon field research conducted during 2022-23 involving a survey of 184 households from two villages in the region. The area under soybean has seen phenomenal increase in two decades, which along with sugarcane cultivation, has led to unsustainable groundwater use. The changes have resulted in inequities largely disfavouring the small farmers. We conclude that the farmers are able to exercise little agency and are primarily responding to external signals in making cropping decisions, resulting in unsustainable resource use and unviable livelihoods.

title: Predicting and explaining electoral support for the far-right in the Netherlands: from Boomers to Zoomers
abstract: This thesis explores whether machine learning models can accurately predict and explain support for far-right parties in the Netherlands, using demographic, economic, and cultural data across different generations. While prior research has linked far-right support to cultural backlash and economic anxiety, most studies rely on linear, descriptive methods that overlook cohort-specific dynamics and limit predictive power. Even among these empirical studies, findings are contested, with ongoing debate over the nature and scope of generational differences in political alignment. To address these gaps, this study applies LightGBM, Random Forest, and Logistic Regression models to predict far-right support, using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) across all models to ensure both high predictive performance and transparent, feature-level interpretation. It draws on harmonized cross-sectional data from the Dutch LISS panel for the 2010 and 2023 elections, and systematically tests how methodological choices—binary versus multiclass classification, as well as the inclusion or exclusion of political proximity variables—affect both prediction accuracy and interpretability. The best-performing model—LightGBM trained on 2023 data with political features—achieved 93% accuracy, an AUC of 0.97, and an F1-score of 0.85, outperforming all other models across every evaluation metric. SHAP results show that leader sympathy became the most salient predictor by 2023, while immigration attitudes were more central in 2010. Contrary to popular claims, younger voters were not uniquely driven by authoritarian or anti-immigrant views, nor were older generations predominantly motivated by cultural backlash. Overall, the study demonstrates how interpretable machine learning can uncover nuanced, non-linear patterns in political behavior— particularly across generational groups—while preserving transparency and reproducibility. This highlights its value as a methodological bridge for the social sciences: one that combines the predictive power of modern ML with the explanatory clarity needed for substantive, theory-driven analysis.

title: Expanding the utility of protest event datasets with automated variable extraction from event summaries
abstract: Previous research shows that civil resistance works. Various event datasets emerged and led to a large body of disaggregated analyses of protest dynamics. Although observations in all event datasets are based on text sources, such as news articles and reports, they provide different and often distinct variables. As a result, scholars with particular research questions and applications are restricted to using one or only a few of these datasets. Many of them are no longer maintained, further restricting applied researchers and other users. However, some datasets provide event summaries for each observation, from which additional variables can be generated. Using the Armed Conflict and Location Event Data, we generate additional variables present in four other datasets with BERT and large language models. We enable enhancing the usage of an existing dataset for new descriptive, explanatory, and predictive applications, testing the robustness of previous and future findings, and ultimately answering previously out of reach research questions due to variable compartmentalization. We contribute to the study of protest and mobilization by showing how natural language processing can be used to reliably expand dataset usage.

title: Grandparental Care and Loneliness across Europe: The Role of Cultural Context
authors: Martin Lakomý, Sunwoo Lee, Merril Silverstein
abstract: Loneliness is a phenomenon associated with older age and linked to lower well-being and other adverse outcomes. While the factors contributing to loneliness and potential remedies for its reduction have received growing attention, little consideration has been given to grandchild caregiving as a meaningful and socially integrative activity that may ameliorate loneliness—despite its potential both to constrain social participation and to enhance it. This study examines the association between grandparental caregiving and loneliness, with specific attention to the role of macro-socio-cultural context within Europe. We use data from individuals aged 50–90 participating in the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe. Within-person fixed-effects modeling across five waves reveals a negative association between the intensity of grandparental care and loneliness. Tests across groups of European countries differentiated by their individualistic and collectivistic orientations reveal that grandparental care is associated with lower loneliness in individualistic countries and with higher loneliness in the most collectivistic countries. Results are discussed in terms of the broader social consequences of grandparenting and are interpreted as consistent with the possibility that caregiving is particularly beneficial in contexts where it is experienced as a more voluntary activity.

title: "Fill Out this Survey": Capabilities and Detection of Agentic Browsers
abstract: Researchers increasingly rely on people to produce data through online interfaces. Agentic browsers create a new challenge for these workflows because they can navigate websites and complete tasks on a user’s behalf with little technical knowledge or effort. We evaluate whether three consumer-facing agentic browsers can complete online surveys and whether recently proposed measures can detect or prevent their use. The agents received only one simple instruction, "Fill out this survey", without detailed prompting or technical optimization. We tested technical screening measures, visible and invisible CAPTCHAs, AI-specific prompt-injection checks, consistency across a longer survey, and the completion of several surveys from a single instruction. The agents completed surveys with little or no user input, maintained assigned demographic profiles, and passed all tested prompt-leaking and jailbreak-style checks. Browser metadata did not reveal automated participation, and invisible reCAPTCHA was consistently passed by some browsers. Visible reCAPTCHA created the strongest barrier, although agents could sometimes solve it or return control to the user. These findings show that widely available AI agents can take over tasks intended for human participants while producing responses that appear coherent and plausible. This raises broader questions about how researchers can verify that supposedly human-generated data were actually produced by humans.

title: Selling the Feeling of Being Understood: Trust, Access, and Power in AI's Marketing Turn
abstract: In one week in July 2026, three leading AI companies publicly defined themselves through one another. SpaceXAI launched Grok 4.5 through comparative performance claims; Anthropic released the cinematic campaign There's hope in hard questions; and OpenAI's CEO mocked that campaign while relocating competition to price, access, and efficiency. This commentary reads the exchange as a relational repertoire of legitimation rather than as three stable corporate identities. Drawing on archived campaign materials, executive posts, corporate statements, and trade coverage from February to July 2026, it distinguishes registers of trust, access, and founder-centred power. These registers are enabled and constrained, though not mechanically determined, by revenue dependencies. Their common object is the user's relation to AI infrastructure. Anthropic's campaign and accompanying Reflect feature go further by marketing and operationalising the experience of being understood, converting a mechanism associated with sycophancy and affective dependence into a corporate asset and a platform-level mode of user governance.

title: AVID Insights: Diverse Paths to College Predisposition and Search
authors: Brian Holzman, Aminah Crawford, Kristian Edosomwan
abstract: AVID is a college access program for students in the “academic middle,” particularly those from socioeconomically and racially marginalized backgrounds. Although research has examined AVID’s association with college enrollment, less is known about its relationship with earlier stages of the college-choice process. Using nationally representative HSLS data, we examine whether AVID participation is associated with students’ expectations of earning a bachelor’s and engagement in key college search activities. We also assess whether these associations vary by race/ethnicity, first-generation status, and family poverty level. AVID participation is positively associated with attending college programs or tours and consulting school counselors. In some cases, these associations are stronger among socioeconomically and racially marginalized students, suggesting AVID may help reduce disparities in access to college information and guidance.

title: "Even in poverty, a Jew is a prince": The press coverage of the deaths of Beitar movement commanders in Eretz Israel
abstract: This qualitative textual analysis examines the journalistic coverage of the deaths of six former Beitar Movement commanders in the land of Israel: Shimshon Unichman (1961), Menachem Arber (1961), Eri Jabotinsky (1969), Binyamin Eliav (1974), Yonah Froehlich (1976) and Moshe Gold (1986), as reported in thirteen Hebraic newspapers. This line of inquiry reveals that while the deaths of these men constituted as notable media events in the revisionist party press, competing daily newspapers relegated the news to the margins, with rather informative, albeit respectful, mentions. Furthermore, the extent of each figure’s integration into Israeli public or political life after their term as Beitar commanders, as well as Eri Jabotinsky’s family lineage, significantly influenced the scope and tone of media coverage. Between the lines, this article also points to the early decline of the political-propaganda press, which often presented a one-dimensional worldvie. In practice, the Israeli press covered the deaths of former Beitar commanders in an informative and respectful manner, portraying them as national pioneers. Even more so, the revisionist press framed them as folk heroes (Unichman), as spokesmen for Ze’ev Jabotinsky (Arber) and as a source of personal and collective pride (Eri Jabotinsky). Coverage of the deaths of Eliav, Froehlich and Gold, however, was considerably more limited due to the closure of revisionist newspapers, Eliav’s ideological distancing from the political right, and Froehlich’s and Gold’s withdrawal from the political and public arenas. At the same time, and without exception, the journalistic coverage emphasized the Beitar ethos of courage, splendor and righteousness of cause.

title: Faker Island. Profiling misinformation sharers on the French Twittersphere using a matching procedure
authors: Manon Berriche, Jean-Philippe Cointet, Anne-Sophie Hacquin, Sacha Altay, Béatrice Mazoyer, Benjamin Ooghe-Tabanou, Hugo Mercier, Dominique Cardon
abstract: What are the distinctive characteristics of misinformation sharers? So far, most studies have focused on the U.S., a two-party system with a highly polarized media landscape, leaving open the question of what misinformation sharers look like in other socio-political contexts. Research has also prioritized testing causal links between cognitive or political variables and misinformation sharing, while paying less attention to fine-grained descriptions of who these users are. To address this gap, we analyze the French Twittersphere using ideological inference methods and a matching procedure. Drawing on four million tweets, we compare 1,907 users who shared at least one URL flagged as false or misleading by fact-checkers with 958 ideologically matched control users who did not. We show that misinformation sharers are more likely to be located at the extremes of the political spectrum, express hostility toward ruling elites and institutions, display political markers in their bios, use pseudonyms, share media content, engage in high-intensity and retweet-oriented activity, and express negative emotions. They also disproportionately circulate topics related to immigration, terrorism, and criticism of mainstream media. However, their language does not indicate lower analytical thinking. By shifting the focus from cognitive vulnerability alone to political self-presentation, anger, and amplification practices, this study contributes to ongoing theoretical debates and calls for further research on the activist practices and party affiliations of misinformation sharers.

title: A Costly Co-Pilot? AI Usage Signals Reduced Morality via Effort Perceptions
abstract: Artificial intelligence has spread rapidly across life domains. While the discourse about AI risks and benefits gained public traction, little is known about interpersonal perceptions of AI users. Across four studies in three countries (N = 1,219), we compared judgments about individuals using AI to complete a task with individuals completing the task without AI assistance. Robust and large effects emerged across samples, indicating lower moral character judgment for AI users, lowered cooperation partner attractiveness, and lower attributed outcome deservingness. All effects were functions of differences in effort perception, indicating that lower perceived effort accounted for the detrimental effects of AI usage. In sum, the use of AI for completing a task was rated considerably more negatively when compared to completing it without AI. We discuss implications and constraints to generalizability and foreshadow potential drifts in perception along the normalization of AI tools.

title: Putting Research Into Context: A Paradigm Shift in Conceptualizing Executive Functions in Classroom Learning
authors: Fake Person, Rebecca Merkley, Dana Miller-Cotto, Megan E. Brunner, Alison T. Miller Singley, Richard L. Bryck, Martin Buschkuehl, Susanne M. Jaeggi, Caitlin Mills, Aubrey Francisco
abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are related to academic performance, but interventions designed to leverage EFs to improve academic outcomes have shown inconsistent results. Academic performance is also subject to layers of personal, social, task-relevant, and cultural contexts, all of which impact students’ EF engagement in any given task. The EF+Math Program explored the potential for EFs to positively impact math achievement by supporting inclusive research and development of EF learning approaches that are contextually embedded and attend to the needs of diverse students. Across a portfolio of projects, researchers, developers, and educators worked collaboratively to co-design and evaluate learning approaches for middle school mathematics classrooms. Here we share examples of our contextualized research, and our updated conceptualizations of EFs arising from shared insights across different contexts. We conclude with calls to action for continuing inclusive research and development to advance insights across, theory, assessment, and intervention in EF research.

title: The Catch-22 of the logocentric box and the Daoist antidote. A Daoistic perspective on language, knowledge, technology, and nature.
abstract: Our contemporary world is confusing because we no longer know where we stand. Are we on the height of progress and human potential, driven by scientific innovation and technological advancement? Or have we descended into unprecedented, self-inflicted ecological crises threatening our survival? While technological progress is undeniable, it is also the main cause of environmental degradation, creating a paradox that challenges modern thought. This cognitive dissonance is sustained by logocentrism, a way of knowing that considers descriptive language, logic, and measurable knowledge as superior, which disconnects us from direct experience of the Living World, nature, through conceptual constructions. As an antidote to this logocentric trap, we turn to Daoist philosophy, offering a perspective that challenges the dominance of logocentric language and thought. Drawing on Masanobu Fukuoka’s natural Way of farming as a living metaphor, we reflect on this paradox and the logocentric ‘box’ while exploring ecological transformation through wu wei. Using metaphorical language and visual ‘windows’ as epistemic openings, we invite readers to move beyond the logocentric boundaries of these pages and reconnect directly with the Living World.

title: A mixed-methods study of University of Bristol researchers’ perceptions and attitudes towards sustainable research practices
authors: Anne-Laure Donskoy, Daniel Major-Smith, Matthew Fackrell, Katie Major-Smith, Patricia Neville, Kate Tilling, Ava Lorenc
abstract: Objective: Universities are increasingly recognised as contributors to the climate crisis but there is little in-depth data on researchers’ understanding and practice. This project explores researcher knowledge and attitudes, barriers and drivers to embedding sustainability within research processes at a single institution, and how to improve the sustainability of research. Design: Mixed-methods case study. Setting: The University of Bristol (UoB), UK. Data collection: Online survey (n=392) and five online qualitative focus groups (n=29). Participants: Staff and students involved in conducting or supporting research at the University. Results: Survey and qualitative results showed high concern about the climate impact of research (72% very or extremely worried about climate change; 57% believe very important to consider sustainability of research). However, barriers and trade-offs preventing engagement and capacity for change, including the complexity of sustainability, reflecting interconnected systemic problems and competing priorities (potential harms to research, limited funding and time and disproportionate effect on early career researchers). The perceived lack of institutional commitment and prioritisation of sustainability was troubling for participants, with accusations of hypocrisy, greenwashing and poor transparency. Survey data show low levels of training, knowledge and support from UoB (only 4% very or extremely familiar with UoB initiatives). Focus group participants were keen to challenge and disrupt research culture to promote more sustainable research practices, and for open, honest, meaningful conversations. Conclusions: Researchers at UoB who took part in our study were keen to make their research more sustainable, but face systemic barriers and competing priorities, and a troubling lack of institutional support, including funding, time, dialogue, sharing information. These issues are likely found across the wider UK university sector, perhaps globally. To achieve universities’ climate commitments - such as net-zero by 2050 - substantial and meaningful change is required. These findings have been integrated into UoB’s University Climate Action Plan to enact this change.

title: Does exposure to information on ethnic minorities’ greater welfare dependency affect attitudes to welfare and welfare recipients? A pre-registered, population-based survey experiment
authors: Thijs Lindner, Willem de Koster, Jeroen van der Waal
abstract: The relationship between ethnic diversity and welfare attitudes has been the subject of much research. However, little is known about how exposure to information on the overrepresentation of ethnic minority individuals among welfare recipients affects attitudes to welfare recipients in general. We scrutinize a potential information exposure effect, and assess two contrasting scenarios, i.e., exposure to aforementioned information might strengthen either negative stereotypes of welfare recipients or the notion that welfare dependency is the result of structural conditions. Additionally, we hypothesize that the former (latter) response is more likely among those with more (less) ethnocentric attitudes. We tested this by conducting an original pre-registered survey experiment among members of a high-quality probability-based panel designed to represent the Dutch population (n = 1,527). The treatment group was exposed to information depicting the overrepresentation of Dutch citizens with a Moroccan migration background among welfare recipients in the Netherlands, while the control group was not. It was only among the more ethnocentric respondents that exposure to the treatment increased support for the notions that welfare recipients: 1) are lacking work ethic; and 2) are themselves to blame for their condition. There was 3) no treatment effect on support for welfare schemes in general. We discuss the implications of these findings for a variety of academic debates and make suggestions for further research.

title: Evolution of cooperation when defectors spread gossip with lies in the population
abstract: Liars permeate society, deceiving and exploiting cooperators, thereby undermining trust and cooperation. As individuals can obtain information about others through social interaction, we propose an evolutionary game model that unifies direct and indirect reciprocities to investigate the conditions necessary for the evolution of cooperation when deceptive gossip spreads. The model explicitly allows individuals to condition their behavior on reputational information and strategically manipulate that information through biased or false gossip. We find two types of lying defectors that evolve more than other possible ones; the GBBG-DEFECTORs, who spread gossip contrary to reputation they obtain about others, and the GGBG-DEFECTORs, who spread good gossip about others indiscriminately regardless of their reputation. Using analytical results and agent-based simulations, we demonstrate that these defectors are defeated by strategic discriminated cooperators (S-DISCs), who prioritize direct game experiences over gossip and ignore gossip about third parties from players with bad reputation, when information spreads rapidly and interactions are repeated. When interacting with lying defectors, S-DISC earns higher payoffs than classical direct reciprocal strategy, Tit-for-Tat, at low benefit-to-cost ratios and under the low game iterations. The population size does not have a significant impact on the evolution of S-DISC even when lying defectors spread lies. Overall, this study provides a general theoretical framework clarifying the conditions under which cooperation can evolve and remain stable when defectors spread lies.

title: PLACING ACCESSIBILITY AT THE CENTER OF TRAVEL BEHAVIOR MODELING: A CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK
authors: Matheus Fontenelle Siqueira, Carlos Felipe Grangeiro Loureiro
abstract: The paradigm shift from mobility to accessibility planning demands analytical approaches to understanding and modeling travel behavior. Yet most behavioral frameworks still lack a clearer representation of how urban form, individual, accessibility, and travel behavior relate to each other; most represent accessibility indirectly through exogenous attributes of the built environment and transport networks, neglecting its temporal, individual and digital components. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that positions accessibility as the central mediator between urban structure and individual travel decisions. Grounded in time geography and building on the multidimensional accessibility model of Geurs and van Wee (2004, 2026), the framework integrates land-use, transport, temporal, individual-and-social, and digital components, and articulates how tangible constraints and perceptions jointly shape travel behavior. The framework is designed to accommodate feedback loops and self-selection mechanisms, providing a structure for both theoretical reflection and empirical analysis. As a proof of concept, we apply it through a multigroup Structural Equation Model to household travel survey data from Fortaleza, Brazil, a highly segregated metropolis. The empirical results support the mediating role of accessibility and reveal gendered differences in how its components translate into motorized and non-motorized mobility. By making explicit the influences of accessibility components on travel behavior, the framework offers researchers and planners a structured basis for hypothesis formulation and for aligning transport modeling with goals of social inclusion, accessibility equity, and sustainable urban development.

title: Certification, Not Transformation: The Performance Signature of Italy's Innovative-Firm Status and Its Regional Contingency
authors: Angelo Leogrande, Mauro di Molfetta, Valeria Nortarnicola, Maria Giovanna Trotta, Nicola Magaletti
abstract: Italy's special legal status for "innovative" small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) grants fiscal, financial and administrative benefits intended to strengthen competitiveness, yet whether the status marks a distinctive profile of realised firm performance remains empirically underexplored. Using ten years of balance-sheet data assembled within the LUCE (LUtech Campus Ecosystem) research project on 4,043 firms (2,873 innovative and 1,170 ordinary), we compare the two populations across six performance dimensions—performance persistence, revenue growth, labour productivity, operating profitability, earnings volatility and financial stability. Because the populations differ systematically in size, sector and location, we use propensity-score matching (1,031 balanced pairs) and interpret the resulting differential as a conditional innovative-status premium rather than as a causal effect. Innovative SMEs display a large and robust revenue-growth premium—a median growth rate roughly three-and-a-half times that of matched ordinary peers (+17.3 percentage points per year; rank-biserial 0.53)—coexisting with a fragility penalty of higher earnings volatility and lower financial stability; operating profitability is higher but does not survive our robustness battery, and labour productivity is marginally lower. A within-firm event study around the registration date shows that the growth advantage largely predates registration, indicating that the status certifies and renders visible already-dynamic firms rather than causally upgrading them. The premium is strongly and significantly heterogeneous across space—broadest in the South, where local institutions are weakest—consistent with an institutional-substitution boundary condition that a formal region-by-status interaction confirms. The results are robust to nine alternative estimators, multiple-testing correction and hidden-bias diagnostics. We read the innovative-firm register as an informative screening and monitoring device rather than as a policy whose causal returns we measure.

title: Value Determinants of Youth Professional Self-Realization (Author's English Translation)
abstract: The article is devoted to the theoretical and empirical analysis of the professional self-realization of students and the definition of its value determinants. According to the author, the professional self-realization of young people is a stage of socialization, where professional potential is formed and realized; it includes a set of professional competencies and special personality traits necessary for the effective implementation of labor activity. Professional self-realization is impossible without the creation of appropriate conditions, which is part of the State Youth Personnel Policy: an institutionally organized socio-managerial activity of the subjects of youth policy aimed at regulating personnel processes in the youth environment of the country. The effectiveness of the organization of personnel processes depends on how much this process responds to the values of youth. To determine the value conditions for the professional self-realization of students, the results of a sociological study were analyzed. The study was conducted in 2022 under the guidance of the author among Russian students (N=18,392). As a result of the analysis, two groups of value determinants of professional self-realization were identified: primary and secondary. Primary value determinants are strategic; they should be considered when building the personnel policy of the organization, and they are in the area of responsibility of the head of the organization; this group includes the value conditions through which respondents reveal the content of self-realization. Secondary value determinants of professional self-realization are tactical. They should form the basis of the adaptation practice for each new employee of the organization and be in the area of responsibility of the immediate supervisor; this group includes the most important value conditions in employment for students who need the opportunity for professional self-realization. The revealed value determinants of professional self-realization can be included in the program of adaptation of young specialists in the organization. title: Social Environment as a Factor in the Changing Values of Student Youth (Author's English Translation)
abstract: This article is devoted to the study of the influence of the social environment and its changes on the values of students. The article says that ensuring adherence to values is a difficult task, including a deep study of the nature of values, the conditions for their formation, as well as the development of measures to ensure sustainable adherence to these values, especially among students. Based on various definitions of values, the article presents the author's operational definition, which became the starting point for the organization of applied sociological research. Based on the conducted factorial and cluster analysis of the sociological research data, typological groups were formed, described through correlation with the heroes of Russian literature. Thanks to the chosen method of typological analysis, it was possible to clearly demonstrate possible changes in the values of student youth under the influence of a changing social environment, and also to describe the likely social trajectories of students as a result of moving away from previous values. The Russian original is the version of record. Archived translation: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21610437

title: Challenges in Environmental Provisions: Toward an Identification of Determinant Factors in Latin American Trade Agreements
authors: Nicolas De la Peña, Irma Liliana Vasquez-Merchan
abstract: International Environmental Agreements (IEAs) and Preferential Trade Agreements (PTAs) are supposed to influence domestic environmental norms. Although recent literature has examined global patterns, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the situation in Latin America. This paper aims to assess the effect of international agreements on domestic environmental law in Latin America. We develop an empirical analysis of the relationship between international agreements and national environmental legislation by combining three datasets: International Environmental Agreements Database (IEADB), Trade & Environment Database (TREND), and Food, Agriculture and Renewable Natural Resources Legislation Database (FAOLEX), to address IEAs, PTAs, and domestic legislation, respectively. Our paper contributes to scientific debates on international political economy because Latin America exhibits particularities regarding the influence of international norms on domestic legislation due to political regime, environmental protectionism, the influence of high-income partners, and the more significant impact of PTAs compared to EIAs.

title: Bad Days, Not Bad Groups: Parasocial Contact, Performance, and Prejudice in the English Premier League
authors: Ala Alrababah, William Marble, Salma Mousa, Alexandra Siegel
abstract: The contact hypothesis rests on a potential paradox: positive outgroup exemplars may be dismissed as exceptional while negative exemplars may be taken as representative. We investigate whether this asymmetry burdens minorities, in the case of parasocial contact with elite athletes in the English Premier League. Drawing on millions of social media posts, newspaper articles, and Fantasy Premier League transfer data, we find no evidence that minority players are punished more harshly for poor performances. Survey experiments among fans and non-fans demonstrate that negative coverage of a minority player reduces perceived typicality, and among those with parasocial ties, increased outgroup tolerance and empathy. We attribute this to parasocial buffering. The voluntary, passion-driven nature of fandoms may encourage observers to individuate outgroup members and respond with compassion. By treating typicality as an outcome rather than a precondition, we find that negative experiences need not reinforce intergroup stereotypes. Parasocial exposure to celebrities may be especially well-suited for reducing prejudice in scalable and ethical ways.

title: Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT): Architectural Identification of a Closed Explanatory System
abstract: This pre-print introduces Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT), a foundational explanatory system describing invariant, non-moral, non-psychological mechanics governing human systems across load, detection, identity, power, and time. DHFT is not an application framework and not a theory-in-progress; it is a closed architectural identification of mechanics already governing behavior across individual, institutional, and civic scales. The system is organized around two co-foundational, non-reducible spines: Dimensional Human Physics (DHP), which defines lawful mechanics of load, constraint, accumulation, movement, and time; and Dimensional Self Architecture (DSA), which models structural identity continuity and stabilization over time. A canon-locked bridge domain, Identity Harmonics, governs lawful coupling between these spines without collapse. A pre-foundational condition domain specifies when mechanics apply at all, prior to cognition or interpretation. DHFT explicitly refuses moral, psychological, intent-based, therapeutic, or regulatory framing. It distinguishes detection from cognition, authorization from authority, and structural admissibility from consent. Non-collapse constraints prevent interpretive, applicative, or narrative backflow into mechanics. Dimensional Human Physics (DHP) defines the lawful structural mechanics of load, capacity, and boundary conditions. Despite its name, “physics” refers to structural mechanics rather than material or biological processes. Dimensional Self Architecture (DSA) defines structural identity persistence and operates as a co-equal, non-reducible domain alongside Dimensional Human Physics (DHP) within DHFT.
