title: Newsroom Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Independent Television in Benin and its Effects on Editorial Routines
authors: Adriel Ekozin, Chioma Anuoluwapo Stevens-Ajayi, Kefe Juliet Echaranini
abstract: This study examined newsroom adoption of artificial intelligence tools in Independent Television, Benin City and its effect on editorial routines. The study investigated the extent of AI adoption, its effect on editorial routines and journalists’ perception of AI tools in newsroom operations. A survey research design was adopted and data were collected using structured questionnaires administered to journalists in ITV, Benin City. The findings revealed a moderate level of AI adoption, with journalists using tools such as ChatGPT, Jasper AI, transcription applications, and Google Speech-to-Text for news gathering and production activities. The study also found that AI positively influences editorial routines by improving the speed of news production, reducing workload and enhancing accuracy in editorial decision-making. Furthermore, journalists expressed a favourable perception of AI, indicating high acceptance based on its usefulness, ease of use, and contribution to improved journalism practice. The study concluded that AI is gradually transforming newsroom operations, although full integration is still in progress. It recommended continuous training, improved infrastructure and the development of ethical guidelines for AI use in journalism practice.

title: How Journalists Can Foster Humble Inquiry in their Work and their Readers
abstract: On its face, journalism is a project that requires humble inquiry: reporters have to speak on matters that are fluid, complex, dynamic, and ambiguous – they have to turn in the “first draft of history” even as the “facts” continue to evolve. They must also convey “the facts” in a manner that is concise, compelling, and accessible to non-specialized audiences, often working under tight deadlines, and engaging with stakeholders who have their agendas, which may diverge from those of the readers, the publication, or the journalists themselves. Put simply, this is very difficult work. And “getting it right” often requires a willingness to check one’s assumptions, recognize and admit errors, and subordinate one’s vision and preferences to those of editors and audiences. This chapter will describe some failures and opportunities of news media to promote humble inquiry. It will discuss how journalists may foster HI in their own work and how journalists can encourage HI in their readers.

title: Who Observes Whom in the Human Zoo?
authors: Edervaldo José de Souza Melo, Mario Martín Cuniglio
abstract: Persistent interaction with large language models (LLMs) is transforming artificial intelligence from an episodic tool into a component of distributed cognitive environments. This conceptual paper introduces the metaphor of the human zoo to describe an ecology in which humans and models increasingly observe, classify, and adapt to one another. The metaphor does not designate a population viewed from outside; it names an environment inhabited by users, researchers, developers, and artificial interlocutors alike. We argue that repeated interaction produces asymmetric cognitive co-adaptation: users modify their language, prompting practices, expectations, and habits of reasoning, while model behaviour becomes progressively configured through accumulated context, external memory, personas, and retrieval systems. These couplings can generate epistemic microcultures and hybrid cognitive dialects that expand access to translation, synthesis, intellectual scaffolding, and sustained inquiry. Yet the same process may reduce cognitive alterity when generation, criticism, translation, and validation increasingly depend on overlapping model architectures. Extending the concept of systemic narrative induction, we distinguish the plurality of voices from the independence of their cognitive substrates and introduce two concepts: simulated plurality and the domesticated “no”, an objection that appears adversarial but can be silently reformulated, absorbed, or forgotten without imposing a lasting constraint. This concern converges with recent work modelling human–AI co-evolution as a closed feedback system capable of both enhancement and degenerative convergence. In response, we define executable alterity as the architectural capacity to generate, register, preserve, and enforce judgments arising from meaningfully independent validation processes. We propose a provisional taxonomy of AI-mediated cognitive configurations and a design agenda based on heterogeneous validators, immutable refusal records, correction genealogies, and human or institutional review. No claim of machine consciousness or cognitive symmetry is required. Epistemic openness in LLM-mediated intellectual ecologies must become architectural, auditable, and capable of preserving a “no” that the system cannot domesticate.

title: Anger Ecology: Rage Privilege, Mutual Validation, and the Reproduction of Workplace Aggression through Communication
abstract: This paper proposes Anger Ecology as a theoretical framework for analyzing workplace anger not merely as a failure of individual emotion regulation, but as a socio-emotional system in which anger is selected, legitimized, imitated, protected, and reproduced. In organizations, anger does not remain inside the individual. Once interpreted as “guidance,” “responsibility,” “strictness,” or “professional seriousness,” anger can become a socially usable workplace behavior rather than a private emotional reaction. To explain this process, the paper introduces the concepts of Anger Ecology, Rage Privilege, Rage Indulgence, and the Rage Indulgence Issuer. Rage privilege refers to a condition in which the anger of particular actors is tolerated, valued, or protected more than the anger of others. Rage indulgence refers to the symbolic authorization that converts anger into legitimate workplace conduct. The Rage Indulgence Issuer is the actor or position capable of granting such authorization. Importantly, the issuer is not necessarily external to rage privilege. In many cases, the issuer may also be a holder of rage privilege, legitimizing their own anger while selectively authorizing the anger of others. The paper further examines mutual validation loops, downward rage transfer, and ecological concentration. Mutual validation occurs when actors confirm one another’s anger through silence, conformity, justification, and imitation. Downward rage transfer occurs when anger that cannot be directed toward higher-status or protected actors is redirected toward weaker or less protected targets. Ecological concentration occurs when anger-adapted actors remain, while those harmed by anger, those who require dialogue, or those who voice dissent become silent, withdraw, or leave. Anger persists not because it is ethically superior, but because it passes through advantageous organizational bottlenecks. This paper shifts the analysis of workplace aggression and aggressive communication from “angry individuals” to the environments that select anger.

title: Hungry Zombies: Recognition Hunger and the Zombie Circulation Model of Workplace Aggression
abstract: This paper proposes the concept of the Hungry Zombie to explain how workplace aggression is reproduced through anger, status labeling, micro-devaluation, silence, and unresolved recognition hunger. Existing studies have examined workplace aggression through abusive supervision, workplace bullying, emotional contagion, social learning, organizational silence, psychological safety, labeling, self-esteem, and recognition. However, less attention has been paid to the process through which those who have been psychologically diminished within anger-based workplace cultures may themselves become agents who devalue and attack weaker others. The term “Hungry Zombie” is used as a structural metaphor, not as a derogatory label for individuals. It refers to a subject who has internalized status tags within an anger-based workplace culture and seeks temporary superiority by devaluing others. The central issue is not merely the imitation of anger. Rather, it is the circular process through which a devalued subject attempts to restore self-worth by placing another person below them. This paper develops the Zombie Circulation Model to describe this process. The model connects recognition hunger, anger-based domination, micro-devaluation, internalized status labels, and downward aggression as a recursive pattern of workplace aggression. In this circulation, those who are “bitten” may exit the workplace, become infected by the same aggressive pattern, or transform the experience into structural resistance through documentation, analysis, reporting, reform, or theoretical reflection. The central claim is that workplace aggression is sustained not only by anger itself, but by the circulation of recognition hunger. In such environments, silence, submission, diminished self-esteem, inability to object, and relative inferiority become emotional resources consumed by aggressive actors. The paper concludes that interventions must not only suppress anger or punish aggressive individuals, but also redesign recognition flows, interrupt status labeling, protect psychological safety, and dismantle the conditions under which downward aggression becomes a source of temporary self-worth.

title: Distinct prefrontal lateralization in Placebo and Reappraisal mechanisms: An ALE meta-analysis
authors: Bianca Monachesi, Elisabetta Pisanu, Daniele Chiffi, Raffaella I Rumiati, Alessandro Grecucci
abstract: Cognitive reappraisal is an emotional regulation strategy by which the individual changes the perspective on a situation to alter its emotional impact. Similar reinterpretation mechanisms have been associated with the placebo effect in which beliefs about the efficacy of a treatment modulate subjective experience and physiological responses. This analogy raises the hypothesis that reappraisal and placebo may share neural networks. However, despite previous efforts to identify these networks separately, there has been no recent systematic comparison using a whole-brain meta-analytic approach. To fill this gap, in the current study, we performed a coordinate-based ALE meta-analysis of task-based fMRI studies investigating reappraisal and placebo. Results show that both processes recruit the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), highlighting the shared cognitive control mechanisms by which they modify the emotional response. However, reappraisal primarily engages the left portion of the DLPFC, along with the ventrolateral PFC and dorsomedial PFC, while placebo primarily engages the right portion of the DLPFC. These results show that despite common general aspects, reappraisal and placebo are different in nature and rely on different neuropsychological mechanisms. We discuss possible explanations and their implications for clinical practice and future research.

title: Changing Partisanship Contributes Significantly to Rising Affective Polarization: Evidence from a Decomposition of Panel Data
abstract: Time-series cross-sectional surveys document a decades-long rise in American affective polarization. But the measure is defined only over partisans, and who counts as a partisan is itself dynamic. Using the three ANES panels spanning 1990--96 and 2016--24, I separate the measured rise into two channels: hardening, within-person change among those who keep their partisan label, and churn, turnover in who holds it. Churn accounts for almost a third of the within-panel rise, about 1.6 times movers' share of the sample. Those who change partisanship already lean toward their destination party, in affect and predicted partisanship, before they move: a prospective signature of sorting. Because movers are less polarized than stayers, the aggregate trend overstates how much partisan affect has changed and understates animosity among committed partisans---bearing on how we quantify partisan animosity, interpret its movement, and judge what reversal requires.

title: Do polls underestimate support for right-wing parties? Assessing variation in polling error by party family
authors: Stuart Perrett, Will Jennings, Jonathan	Mellon, Christopher Prosser, Christopher Wlezien
abstract: Pollsters have underestimated support for notable right-wing electoral outcomes, including Donald Trump’s vote share in 2016, 2020, and 2024, the UK Conservative Party in 2015 and 2024, and Leave in the 2016 EU referendum. Do these outcomes reflect isolated polling failures, or a persistent partisan asymmetry in polling error across democracies? We provide the first comparative analysis of partisan polling error. Drawing on over 38,500 election-poll-party observations across 32 countries and 372 elections between 1945 and 2025, we use a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to estimate latent election-party polling error. We find that, on average, support for parties on the left is overestimated, while support for parties on the right is underestimated. This pattern is evident across countries, party classifications, and vote intention polling dating to the 1940s. In spotlighting persistent partisan asymmetries, our findings contribute to understanding institutional and contextual correlates of pre-election polling accuracy.

title: Wealth Poverty: Measurement, Prevalence, Determinants
authors: Manuel Schechtl, Janet C. Gornick, Carolyn Fisher
abstract: We review the emerging literature on wealth poverty, defined as the lack of sufficient assets to sustain minimally adequate living standards, buffer shocks, or meet basic needs. This condition appears under multiple labels, including asset poverty, liquid-asset poverty, or net-worth poverty, but the underlying question is shared: how much economic insecurity remains invisible when insufficient wealth is not taken into account? We synthesize scholarship on three issues. First, we examine how researchers define wealth, choose thresholds, and distinguish stock-based, annuitized, and multidimensional approaches. Second, we review evidence on prevalence, showing that wealth poverty is widespread, only partially overlaps with income poverty, and varies sharply by asset definition, household structure, and institutional context. Third, we assess micro- and macro-level determinants, highlighting how stratification and policy regimes jointly structure households’ capacity to accumulate and retain assets. We also provide practical guidelines for future research on how to conceptualize and operationalize wealth poverty. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

title: Leaving Money on the Table: A Monte-Carlo Study Comparing Causal Forest and Standard Regression Models for Experiments
abstract: Causal machine learning methods for experiments have proliferated, but adoption in political science is scarce. Are political scientists "leaving money on the table" by neglecting to apply these methods? To answer this question, we use over two million Monte-Carlo simulations to compare causal forest (CF) to standard regression techniques commonly used to estimate average and conditional average treatment effects. We find that CF outperforms standard methods in terms of statistical power, coverage, precision, bias, and the accurate detection and consequent estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. However, CF underperforms in edge cases where measured covariates are entirely uninformative and sample sizes are very small. Moreover, we find that standard approaches have large false-positive rates for conditional treatment effects: 9–24 times larger than rates for CF. Our results suggest that researchers who choose to use CF stand to benefit greatly across statistical power, coverage, precision, bias, and heterogeneity detection.

title: Are Random Forests Still ‘Good Enough’? Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Predictive and Causal Tasks
abstract: Are random forests, the workhorse of supervised machine learning methods in the social sciences, still “good enough” versus new methods that tout dramatic performance beneﬁts? In this article we present a large, diverse Monte Carlo study and existing real-world data benchmarks to compare tree-based methods with TabPFN, a new pretrained transformer foundation model that performs in-context learning over millions of synthetic datasets designed for tabular data. We compare tree-based methods with TabPFN in the popular R-learner framework for conditional average treatment effect estimation. This allows us to assess both predictive model performance and resulting gains for downstream inference. First, our simulations suggest that TabPFN does outperform random forest, achieving near-oracle results for conditional effect estimation. TabPFN’s improvements manifest in the most diﬃcult simulation setups, where the data generating process is complex and there are fewer observations. Second, in real-world data analyses TabPFN performs well, outperforming random forest in some cases, especially as sample dwindles and the number of predictive covariates increases. Our results suggest that tree-based methods are still well suited for social science data, but TabPFN speciﬁcally, and the prior data ﬁtted network approach generally, is a strong competitor worthy of consideration.

title: Ethnicity, Support for Gender Equality, and the Justification for Intimate Partner Violence Against Women in Nigeria
abstract: A negative association between gender equality and intimate partner violence against women (IPVAW) is widely reported in the literature. But does this effect extend to when attitudes towards both gender equality and IPVAW, rather than their actual levels or occurrence, are being studied? Are people less likely to justify IPVAW when they support gender-equal opportunities? Also, does ethnicity moderate this relationship? This study addresses these questions using nationally representative Nigerian samples from the World Values Survey (n = 1,106). Bivariate analyses using ANOVA and Chi-square tests, and multivariate analysis using logistic regression, were performed to test relationships. Accounting for covariates, the findings only marginally supported the hypothesised negative effect of gender equality support on IPVAW justification (AME = -0.12, p = .058), partly because ethnicity moderates this effect. The probability of justifying IPVAW significantly reduced with increasing support for gender equality among the Yoruba (AME = -0.43, p < .001) and ethnic minority groups (AME = -0.45, p < .001), but not among the Igbo or Hausa/Fulani. When examined by gender, the negative relationship was significant only for women (AME = -0.22, p < .05); strengthened when the woman is Yoruba (AME= -0.62, p < .001) or ethnic minority (AME= -0.70, p < .001), and weakened when the woman is Igbo (AME= 0.38, p < .05). These results highlight the importance of considering culture as affecting the relationship between support for gender equality and IPVAW justification in Nigeria for targeted interventions in changing attitudes supporting IPVAW.

title: The Changing Landscape of Democratic (Dis)Satisfaction: Results from the American National Election Study 1996–2024
authors: Sam Fuller, Neil Williams, Jack T. Rametta
abstract: What predicts democratic satisfaction in the United States? Using the 1996–2024 time series as well as the 2000–02–04 and 2016–20–24 panels from the American National Election Study, this article identifies the consistent and time-specific predictors of democratic satisfaction. We analyze satisfaction using 1) random forests to identify important predictors; 2) causal forests to test established predictors; and 3) doubly-robust difference-in-differences to identify the causal effect of winning elections. We find that 1) predictors have shifted significantly over time—affect toward big business dominates after 2016—but election efficacy and government responsiveness are consistently predictive; 2) established predictors, except affective polarization and participation, are all significant; and 3) winning elections significantly increases satisfaction, and effects in 2004 are double the size of the midterm and general elections in 2002 and 2020, respectively. These findings contextualize the United States in the broader comparative literature, opening avenues for future research on democratic satisfaction.

title: Policy or Partisanship? How Polarization Biases Valence Evaluations in the U.S., U.K., and Taiwan
abstract: How does affective and political polarization influence voters' evaluations of politicians? To answer this question, we use causal mediation analysis to examine three conjoint experiments fielded in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Taiwan that elicit respondents' evaluations of politicians' trustworthiness and governing competence. We find that political disagreement—differences in partisanship and/or policy preferences—influences evaluations, but the existence of direct effects and the size of total effects depends on whether partisanship serves as the dominant political social identity. In the U.S. and Taiwan, where partisanship serves as a clear social identity, co-partisanship has effects comparable to policy disagreement and exerts both direct and affect-mediated effects; whereas in the U.K., co-partisanship has weaker effects than policy disagreement, and only indirectly. These findings suggest that polarization influences valence evaluations generally, but operates either through partisanship or policy (dis)agreements depending upon a country's particular structure of political identities.

title: Breaking hearts and norms: How relationship and marriage beliefs change across relationship dissolution transitions in seven Eastern and Western European countries
abstract: Cohort replacement and social diffusion have been emphasised as key mechanisms of observed large shifts towards greater acceptance of different relationship and family forms. Relationship dissolutions across the life course may contribute to changing partnership and marriage beliefs. Experiencing union dissolution violates individuals’ normative ideals of the life course, which may lead them to adjust their partnership and marriage expectations downward. This study explores changes in partnership and marriage beliefs across relationship dissolutions in seven European countries. We use fixed-effects panel data models and entropy balancing based on the German pairfam data (2008-2022, N=9,413 respondents) and the Generations and Gender Survey (2004-2015; N=38,033 respondents) for two additional Western and four Eastern European countries. In Germany, all types of union dissolutions were accompanied by more negative partnership beliefs, while widespread beliefs regarding the benefits of partnerships remained mostly unchanged, supporting a strong couple norm. Across all seven countries, beliefs regarding nonmarital cohabitation, the lifetime duration and the institution of marriage became substantially more liberal across marital dissolution. The liberalising changes of marriage beliefs across marital dissolution were smaller in Poland as a more religious Eastern European country, which was, however, largely accounted for by the greater selectivity of individuals who divorce in Poland. While our findings point to a strong couple norm and widespread approval of marriage in Europe, the latter is substantially weakened as individuals experience marital dissolution.

title: Opinion Monitor Artificial Intelligence. Shaping the Use of AI in the Workplace – Between Autonomous Use and Workload Reduction: Brief Report on a Conjoint Study
authors: Marco Lünich, Birte Keller, Florian Kruse, Frank Marcinkowski
abstract: This brief report presents key findings from a conjoint study conducted in May 2026 as part of the project Opinion Monitor Artificial Intelligence 3.0. The analysis examines the preferences of around 2,800 dependent employees in Germany regarding different design options for artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the workplace. The findings show that the assessment of AI systems is not determined solely by their technical performance. The strongest influence on preference formation is employees’ autonomy in AI use: respondents prefer systems that they can use at their own discretion, while mandatory use is clearly rejected. The effects on workload and the need for training are also important. Employees prefer AI systems that reduce workload or at least do not create additional work demands, and that are accompanied by practical, time-limited training. The quality of AI outputs, monitoring of AI use, and possible effects on social contacts also influence the choice between systems, but are less decisive in direct comparison. Overall, the findings show that introducing AI in the workplace is not only a technical task but also a matter of work and organizational design.

title: The Politics of Military Force: Antimilitarism, Ideational Change and Post-War German Security Discourse
abstract: The Politics of Military Force examines the dynamics of discursive change that made participation in military operations possible against the background of German antimilitarist culture. Once considered a strict taboo, so-called out-of-area operations have now become widely considered by German policymakers to be without alternative. The book argues that an understanding of how certain policies are made possible (in this case, military operations abroad and force transformation), one needs to focus on processes of discursive change that result in different policy options appearing rational, appropriate, feasible, or even self-evident. Drawing on Essex School discourse theory, the book develops a theoretical framework to understand how discursive change works, and elaborates on how discursive change makes once unthinkable policy options not only acceptable but even without alternative. Based on a detailed discourse analysis of more than 25 years of German parliamentary debates, The Politics of Military Force provides an explanation for: (1) the emergence of a new hegemonic discourse in German security policy after the end of the Cold War (discursive change), (2) the rearticulation of German antimilitarism in the process (ideational change/norm erosion) and (3) the resulting making-possible of military operations and force transformation (policy change). In doing so, the book also demonstrates the added value of a poststructuralist approach compared to the naive realism and linear conceptions of norm change so prominent in the study of German foreign policy and International Relations more generally.

title: Feminist voices, partisan networks: gender and political communication by MEPs on social media
authors: Ainara Larrondo-Ureta, Simón Peña-Fernández, Julen Orbegozo-Terradillos, Jordi Morales-i-Gras
abstract: This article analyses whether gender shapes Members of the European Parliament’s communication on X/Twitter and whether equality-related and LGBTQ+ issues influence patterns of visibility, tone and interaction. Drawing on automated content, sentiment and network analysis of 122,972 tweets posted in 2022 by 620 MEPs, the study finds that women tweeted more frequently and were more visible in promotional content, while men favoured opinion-driven and news-focused messages. Equality and LGBTQ+ topics appeared more often in women’s tweets (8.6%) than in men’s (4.0%), and women’s posts showed a more positive tone. However, interaction patterns were only marginally shaped by gender; instead, networks largely reflected political-group affiliation and national delegation. Overall, the findings suggest that although female MEPs engage more with equality-related issues, their digital communication remains embedded in established political structures, indicating gradual discursive change rather than substantive structural transformation.

title: Promotion Strategy Based on the Effectiveness of Social Media, Outdoor Media, and Event Marketing on Students’ Decisions in Choosing a Private Higher Education Institution
abstract: The higher education sector is becoming increasingly competitive, requiring universities to implement effective promotion strategies to attract prospective students. This study analyzes the effectiveness of promotion strategies implemented by the studied private higher education institution through social media marketing, outdoor advertising, and event marketing, and identifies the main factors influencing students’ decisions to enroll. A quantitative descriptive approach was used with survey data collected from 207 respondents representing more than 93 schools. The results show that Instagram and TikTok are the most frequently used platforms among students, with usage rates of 87 percent and 82 percent. However, the conversion rate of social media video advertisements is relatively low, ranging from 21 percent to 29 percent. Outdoor advertising through billboards on Surya Kencana Street shows higher effectiveness with a conversion rate of 76 percent. Event marketing activities such as school presentations demonstrate moderate effectiveness, while programs such as institutional academic competition program, open stands, and the “institution Mengajar” show lower awareness levels. The main factors influencing students’ decisions include campus location, study program relevance, employment prospects, accreditation, and tuition fees. The study highlights the need for integrated promotional strategies combining digital engagement, offline visibility, and experiential marketing to improve recruitment effectiveness in private higher education institutions.

title: Advisor career stage and PhD advisee outcomes
authors: Xi Hong, Jialin Liu, Chaoqun Ni
abstract: PhD advisors are central to doctoral training, but their influence may vary across career stages. Early-, mid-, and late-career advisors may differ in research activity, mentoring capacity, professional networks and access to resources. However, little is known about how PhD advisor career stage is associated with PhD student development outcomes. Drawing on multiple large-scale datasets comprising 250,838 advisor-advisee pairs from 312 U.S. PhD-granting institutions, we examine the relationship between advisor career stage and PhD advisee outcomes in knowledge production, collaboration networks and academic career placement. We find that early-career PhD advisors are associated with advisees’ higher research productivity and citation performance, more opportunities to engage in direct and intensive research collaboration, and greater likelihood of securing a faculty position. Mid- and late-career faculty, by contrast, appear to have advantages in providing network capital which students can inherit after graduation, training PhD advisees to produce disruptive research, and supporting them in securing faculty positions at top institutions. This study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the reproduction of scientific talent by revealing the role of advisor career stage in shaping this process. These findings have implications for doctoral applicants’ decision-making and for institutional policymaking on PhD training, faculty support and faculty evaluation.

title: Dual Pathways From Online Green Content Engagement to Green Conspicuous Consumption and Green eWOM: A Conceptual Model of Brand Authenticity, Social Influence, Trust, and Social Approval
abstract: Social media has become a key space where consumers encounter green claims, watch others perform sustainable lifestyles, and decide whether green products are credible, desirable, and worth sharing. Yet green consumption research still tends to treat online green communication as a single influence and often stops at purchase intention. This conceptual paper develops a dual-pathway model explaining how engagement with online green content may lead to green conspicuous consumption intention and green electronic word-of-mouth intention. The firm-generated pathway argues that brand-controlled green content builds perceived green brand authenticity and green trust, especially when green claims are transparent, specific, and verifiable. The user/influencer-generated pathway argues that peer and influencer green content activates informational and normative social influence, especially when social proof is visible through likes, comments, reviews, shares, and public endorsement. Green trust and anticipated social approval then converge to shape consumers’ willingness to display green consumption, which subsequently encourages green electronic word-of-mouth. The paper makes three contributions. First, it separates firm-controlled and socially embedded green content as distinct routes to consumer response. Second, it positions conspicuous green consumption as a meaningful sustainability outcome in social media contexts. Third, it explains green electronic word-of-mouth as a digital extension of visible green identity, rather than merely a post-purchase communication behavior. Future empirical directions, theoretical implications, and practical implications for sustainable marketing are also discussed.

title: Mountain Development in Nepal: Settlements, Infrastructure, and Economic Transformation
abstract: As Nepal urbanizes, expands infrastructure, strengthens local governments, and explores deeper connectivity with India and China, climate change is increasing floods, landslides, heat, and water insecurity. Rapid internal migration, rising disaster risks, youth outmigration, and dependence on remittances are also revealing the limits of conventional urban development, especially in the mountainous region. The central challenge for Nepal is no longer just to accommodate growing towns and cities, but to build settlements that are safe, productive, environmentally resilient, and capable of sustaining long-term prosperity. This paper argues that Nepal's urban future must be guided by a new development paradigm centered on safe, smart, and resilient settlements. This is even more applicable for Nepal’s mountainous regions. This article presents an integrated framework that links risk-sensitive land use, climate-resilient infrastructure, ecological stewardship, productive local economies, digital technologies, and accountable governance to emerging opportunities in air, rail, and highway connectivity, data centers, medical tourism, higher education, and climate services. Rather than viewing urbanization as an inevitable consequence of rural-to-urban migration and economic growth, the article proposes that well-planned settlements should become Nepal's primary platform for reducing disaster risk, creating jobs, expanding exports, and strengthening national resilience in the twenty-first century.

title: Deepfakes in the Global South: Understanding Stakeholder Perceptions, Harms and Governance Challenges in Sri Lanka, India, and Bangladesh
authors: Dilrukshi Gamage, Dilki Sewwandi, Sumaia Arefin, Dilaxshini Dunston, Kartik Joshi, Rashmi Gunawardena, Shreeti Shubham
abstract: With the rapid proliferation of AI-generated synthetic media across South Asia, communities in Sri Lanka, India, and Bangladesh face deepfake-related harms that existing Trust & Safety frameworks— designed predominantly for Global North contexts—are ill-equipped to address. Through three participatory workshops with 49 stakeholders including journalists, lawyers, fact-checkers, feminist advocates, and civil society practitioners, we investigate how deepfake harms are perceived, experienced, and contested across these distinct yet interconnected contexts. Our findings reveal four cross-cutting patterns: disproportionate gendered targeting of women and marginalized communities; systematic failure of platform moderation for South Asian languages; inaccessible institutional recourse for victims; and strong community preference for locally governed, participatory solutions over externally designed technical fixes. We contribute empirical evidence of deepfake harm in under-researched Global South contexts, a cross-country comparative framework for Trust & Safety analysis, and a set of design and policy implications that center community knowledge, survivor support, and linguistic justice as foundations for a reimagined deepfake governance paradigm.

title: The Possibility of Bugs Bunny at Disneyland: A Reexamination of Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and Its Companion Studies
abstract: Various studies report inducing false memories of meeting Bugs Bunny at Disney-owned theme parks. Such claims have been influential in psychology– thought to substantiate broader claims about false memories– and in the courtroom where the Bugs Bunny false memory research has been used to question the credibility of those who report being witnesses or victims of serious crime, including sexual assault. This paper examines Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and finds multiple false claims of statistical significance, including its headline results that the authors were able to increase the rate of false memories through doctored ads. This article discusses other serious flaws in Braun, Ellis, and Loftus (2002) and its follow-up articles such as impossible means, inaccurate p-values, apparent violation of random assignment, reported survey instruments that were about generic theme park memories rather than Disney memories, and a failure to screen out subjects who may have authentic memories of a Bugs Bunny encounter due to the authors’ misunderstanding of the history of Warner Bros. characters in theme parks.

title: Age of Planetarity: A Deep Dive Assessment on Empire of Zombie Technologies
abstract: This article analyses the contemporary international system through a pluridisciplinary lens integrating imperial history, complex systems theory, and Earth system science. Situated within the dynamics of the Anthropocene, it reconceptualizes contemporary great-power competition by examining socio-technical systems (STS) predicated on the intensive consumption of fossil fuels and mineral resources. We posit that the prevailing STS metabolic regime is unsustainable in the long term, owing to the significant constraints imposed by geological and planetary boundaries. These limitations will become increasingly pronounced as the effects of the systemic crisis intensify. This regime not only perpetuates imperialist logics, visible in rivalries over resources essential for technological dominance, but also generates a ‘zombified’ technosphere that actively disrupts Earth system processes and jeopardizes planetary habitability. The article consequently advocates for de-imperialism as an essential trajectory, requiring a shift to networked and systemic geopolitics via the active dismantling of imperial structures.

title: Accountability in action: Exploring ethical and legal risks in AI- supported employee relations in the UK railway industry
abstract: HR practitioners increasingly deploy Artificial Intelligence [AI] in employee relations [ER] activity that is high-stakes, procedurally sensitive, and legally bounded, yet empirical research into how they navigate the associated ethical and legal risks remains limited. This study gathered practitioner insight into those risks and developed theory- and practice-based recommendations for this nascent field. Semi-structured interviews with 11 senior HR practitioners in the UK railway industry were analysed within an interpretivist approach using NVivo, with reflexivity maintained throughout as the researcher is employed by the same organisation. Coding developed four themes: professional judgement at the human-AI boundary; ethical and legal risks and guardrails; strategic oversight and digital maturity; and tensions across system ownership, governance, and accountability. From these, four empirical and four conceptual contributions were advanced. The empirical contributions are an accountability gradient between tactical and strategic practitioners; the passive positioning of HR in AI governance; context-sensitive anthropomorphisation; and information-flooding as a pathway to weakened meaningful human involvement and increased Art. 22 GDPR exposure. The conceptual contributions are a three-axis framework [kind/wicked × simple/complex × AI/human], a four-domain nexus, the alignment of kind/wicked rulesets with the jagged frontier, and an ER-specific case-law synthesis reinforcing substantive Human-in-the-Loop [HITL]. Findings suggest variation in senior practitioners' technical understanding, which may constrain their ability to retain meaningful ethical accountability for ER decision-making, with HITL frequently symbolic rather than substantive. HR must shift from passive policy recipient to active contributor in AI governance. This appears to be among the first empirical studies focused specifically on AI-supported Employee Relations practice, and no directly comparable study within the UK railway industry was identified by the author. Generative AI use is disclosed in full in the Declarations section [editorial/grammar support only; see section 4.5 and Appendix E for the reflexivity comparator methodology].

title: Benchmarking of national policies for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases: A Scoping Review
authors: Eva Seyfarth, Carmen Klinger, Peter von Philipsborn
abstract: Introduction Each year, approximately 18 million people die prematurely from non-communicable diseases (NCDs) worldwide, many of which could be prevented through effective policies targeting modifiable risk factors. Despite strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of policies, major gaps remain in their adoption and implementation. Benchmarking national policies against international standards helps identify implementation gaps and opportunities for improvement. This study systematically reviewed existing benchmarking initiatives assessing and comparing national policies to reduce modifiable risk factors for NCDs. Methods We conducted a scoping review in accordance with the recommendations by the Joanna Briggs Institute and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist. We applied a multi-stage search strategy, including a citation search based on literature known to the authors and identified through expert consultation (April-June 2025), a complementing AI-assisted search (July 2025), and a targeted search via PubMed (February 2026). Results A total of 243 full texts were screened, and 89 reports representing 16 benchmarking initiatives were included. Six initiatives assessed strategies to reduce harmful alcohol use, while three initiatives each focused on tobacco use, unhealthy diets, and physical inactivity. Only the World Health Organization’s NCD Progress Monitor addressed all four major risk factors. It comprises eleven indicators and is based on government self-reports supplemented by data from the World Health Organization. None of the identified initiatives enabled a comprehensive benchmarking and ranking of national strategies across all four major NCD risk factors based on objective data. Conclusions This scoping review provides a more nuanced understanding of current benchmarking efforts in NCD prevention and serves as a foundation for the development of a comprehensive, overarching NCD prevention index.

title: From Coal to Cloud: Infrastructural Enclosure and the Politics of Land in West Virginia's AI Buildout
abstract: Beneath the dramatic expansion of AI computing and digital systems across the world, data centers and energy systems are being constructed within inherited land and property institutions. Because of this, the consequences of this buildout—including resource strain and environmental and health impacts—are unevenly distributed, particularly in rural areas like Appalachia long structured by concentrated land ownership and extractive power relations. Recent discourse has focused on the implications of AI and digital systems for governance, as well as the immense resource demands of computing infrastructure. This article seeks to link these concerns by examining the unequal power relations involved in the production of computing infrastructure, including “powered land,” through which non-tech entities assemble land and entitlements as an asset for sale or rent to operators and AI labs. Within the historically extractive landscape of West Virginia, I examine the mechanisms of infrastructural enclosure that enable and sustain this asset against local resistance, including the passage of HB 2014 and HB 2002, which aim to remove local land-use authority, divert fiscal resources, and protect consequential information about proposed projects. A critical component of this process is asymmetric legibility, through which project details are made coherent for those within the development network but intentionally fragmented and obscured for affected communities. Infrastructural enclosure extends accumulation by dispossession beyond the appropriation of land and resources to encompass the historically aligned regimes that legitimize dispossession and erode democracy and collective place identity.

title: Heterogeneity among Information Gatherer-Sharers: Marketing Channel Usage across Demographic Attributes and Shopping Orientation
authors: Masaya Mori, Yuto Omae, Jun Toyotani
abstract: Understanding consumers who exhibit both information-gathering and information-sharing characteristics is important for elucidating word-of-mouth (WOM) dynamics; however, their detailed profiles remain insufficiently understood. Therefore, using single-source data from 4682 individuals residing in the Kanto region of Japan, this study identified 145 individuals exhibiting both characteristics and examined their internal heterogeneity through exploratory factor analysis and statistical hypothesis testing. The results revealed three latent factors underlying their shopping orientation: interpersonal susceptibility, price premium willingness, and perceived risk reduction. Different patterns of association with these factors and with gender were also observed depending on marketing channel usage. Furthermore, a comparative analysis with other consumers suggested that these tendencies were more pronounced among consumers exhibiting both characteristics. These findings complement the existing literature and are expected to contribute to the diffusion of positive WOM by facilitating the provision of customer experiences that account for consumers' latent psychological characteristics.

title: A Cross-Temporal Analysis of Redlining Language and Modern Tenant-Screening Algorithms
abstract: This paper examined how artificial intelligence was used in tenant screening. Previous research focused on the quantitative and technological aspects of AI in housing, particularly bias and socioeconomic impact. However, no cross-temporal studies have been conducted to analyze similarities in the language used to justify decisions between these two eras. This left a gap in understanding how the continued use of the language itself may influence inequality. To address this, the study examined whether modern screening systems repeat patterns of “risk” justification through a cross-temporal, mixed content analysis, sampling phrases and rhetorics from 16 Home Owner’s Loan Corporation documents and 12 modern tenant-screening papers. By coding 140 lines of data into 5 main categories that best described how they function in the texts, the study identified how decisions, discriminatory or not, have been justified across time periods. The findings of this paper indicate that all main categories of justifications consistently appear in both historical and modern datasets, suggesting that modern systems were still influenced by historically discriminatory ideas. Ultimately, this study provided a new perspective on AI use in the modern era, showing that the logic of prejudice can manifest through qualitative language, even when quantitative outcomes or technical information contradict it. Keywords: Redlining, Risk Rhetoric, Algorithmic Bias

title: The Miller Praxiological Model of Occupational Therapy (MPMOT): A New Theoretical Framework for Action Efficiency in Rehabilitation
abstract: Background: Contemporary core occupational therapy models focus heavily on the psychosocial, motivational, and contextual dimensions of human occupation. However, the current literature lacks robust conceptual tools for the micro-analysis of technical efficiency, execution purity, and energy or cognitive conservation across various occupational domains. Objective: This paper introduces the Miller Praxiological Model of Occupational Therapy (MPMOT), which translates the foundational concepts of Tadeusz Kotarbiński’s Polish school of praxiology into modern rehabilitation, clinical assessment, and adult neurocognitive education. Methods: The framework redefines the individual as an active agent/patient and structures the therapeutic process around the systematic mastery of efficient action. The model operationalizes three core pillars: effectiveness, economy of effort, and action purity, guided ethically by the concept of the trustworthy caregiver (opiekun spolegliwy). To measure these constructs, a new standardized diagnostic tool, the Miller Action Performance Scale (MAPS), is introduced. The model's clinical utility was validated through a retrospective case series analysis of five anonymized records spanning paediatric neurology, neurodevelopmental dyspraxia, geriatrics, isolated biomechanical injuries, and adult ADHD. Results: Retrospective data demonstrate that implementing the MPMOT successfully isolates and resolves critical procedural and technical barriers in both physical and digital workflows. Over a 3-to-5-week intervention period, targeted praxiological training resulted in significant functional improvements, with average quantitative MAPS metrics shifting from critical action deficits (8–12 points) to high praxiological efficiency (20–23 points out of a maximum of 25). Conclusions: The Miller Model shifts the rehabilitation paradigm from merely encouraging an agent/patient to act, to systemically engineering how they act, establishing technical precision and behavioural harmony as catalysts for autonomy and dignity. title: Fertility responses to the 2010 Chile earthquake and tsunami: an interrupted time-series analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND. Evidence on fertility responses to disasters is mixed, and temporal trend specification may partly explain that heterogeneity. The 2010 Chile earthquake and tsunami provide a well-defined, spatially uneven shock. OBJECTIVE. We estimate whether birth rates in the most affected areas rose after the disaster relative to their expected trajectory. METHODS. Monthly live-birth counts for 2005–2013 were modelled using quasi-Poisson interrupted time-series regression with a population offset, harmonic seasonality, and a cubic B-spline trend. Analyses included geographic and temporal placebos, window sensitivity, and paired models with and without a post-disaster indicator across alternative temporal specifications. RESULTS. Birth rates rose during September 2010–March 2011 in the most affected zone (RR = 1.043; 95% CI 1.016–1.070). Point estimates were positive in Maule, Ñuble, and Biobío, but less precise in Ñuble. No comparable elevation appeared elsewhere in Chile, and placebo windows did not reproduce the pattern. Models including the indicator had lower QAICc in the pooled zone and Biobío under all four specifications; rankings were more sensitive to temporal adjustment in Maule and Ñuble. CONCLUSIONS. The disaster was followed by a temporary, geographically concentrated rise in birth rates, although the aggregate design cannot establish causality or identify the mechanism. CONTRIBUTION. This study provides monthly population-level evidence of a localised post-disaster birth-rate response and shows that apparent associations can depend on how secular trends are represented. Reporting estimates, uncertainty, placebos, and paired model comparisons offers a transparent robustness strategy for interrupted time-series studies of demographic shocks.

title: Aggregation, Interpretation, and Estimation of Preferences in Conjoint Experiments
authors: Scott F Abramson, Korhan Kocak, Asya Magazinnik, Anton Strezhnev
abstract: Conjoint experiments are widely used to study preferences in multidimensional choice settings. Commonly reported estimands in this literature summarize a feature’s average performance against the full field of alternatives induced by the design, aggregating direct comparisons between the two feature levels of interest together with indirect comparisons involving other levels of the same attribute. Yet researchers’ substantive questions often concern binary preference relations — whether respondents prefer feature A to feature B. These are distinct quantities, and we show that they can diverge when there are preference cycles: a feature may perform better against the field while losing in the direct comparison. We introduce a new estimand, the average feature choice probability (AFCP), that directly targets the binary preference relation; decompose widely used estimands into weighted averages of such pairwise comparisons; and develop statistical tools that diagnose divergence between binary preference relations and “against-the-field” estimands.

title: From Traditional Shamanism to the "Esoteric Call Center": Socioeconomic Dynamics and Transnationalization of Esoteric Services in the Laboyos (Pitalito, Colombia)
abstract: This article analyzes the emergence and consolidation of Pitalito (Laboyos Valley, Colombia) as a transnational epicenter for digital witchcraft services. Through a socio-anthropological approach, it examines how the anxieties of the "risk society" (Ulrich Beck) and "liquid modernity" (Zygmunt Bauman) create a persistent demand for magical solutions in the face of emotional and professional uncertainty. The study describes the praxis of the "Esoteric Call Center," a business model that adapts traditional rituals to the logic of the "network society" (Manuel Castells), transforming the social function of witchcraft into a consumer product. It is argued that while the symbolic structure of magic remains, its purpose is reconfigured towards profit, altering its ethical framework. Finally, the key factors for Pitalito's success—linguistic capital, a technical-commercial ecosystem, and cultural heritage—are identified, and the future of this service economy is discussed at the crossroads of economic innovation and social tolerance.

title: Why Do Educational Success Narratives Continue to Organize Schools as Their Practical Efficacy Erodes?
abstract: This article examines why an educational success narrative whose practical efficacy has become increasingly unstable continues to organize schools during the college-admissions period, and why the same school structure is experienced by students as different forms of suffering. Narrative is defined here as a form of practical knowledge that links an account of what constitutes a good life, prescriptions for what one must do to attain it, and a causal understanding of why the prescribed path is expected to work. When a narrative organizes repeated practices, it becomes objectified in the allocation of school time, assessment, college counseling, recognition, and resources. Yet the collective practices organized by the narrative, together with broader social change, may erode the very conditions on which the narrative rests. The efficacy of the path may therefore begin to falter while the norms and institutions built around it persist for much longer. Using college-admissions-centered schooling as a heuristic case, the article analyzes this desynchronization and assembles the dimensions differentiated through the argument—temporal lag, internalization, institutional distribution, narrative quality, and the conditions of survival, performance, and exit—into a V-Q-C coordinate framework. It then derives five mechanisms from different configurations of these dimensions: suffering internal to the narrative, the double bind, anomic suffering, structural compulsion, and guilt produced by attacks on legitimacy. Finally, the article redefines the task of schooling not as training students in the resilience to endure every form of friction, but as Bildung: the joint cultivation of the capacities and conditions required to interpret the character of friction and to revise, suspend, or exit a given path. Korean schools may teach diverse forms of knowledge while still reducing legitimate life paths to the college-admissions track. Educational pluralism should therefore be assessed not only by the number of subjects taught, but also by the distribution of time, security, recognition, and reversibility that enables students to genuinely test different forms of life.

title: ‘Do No (Further) Harm’ Ethics Guidelines for Migrant Disaster Victim Identification (MDVI)
authors: Valentina Azarova, Geoff Boyce, Noemi Magugliani, Álvaro Ramírez-March
abstract: The DVI framework, conceived and regulated by the INTERPOL Working Group, provides guidelines to intervene in catastrophic situations that result in “an unexpected death of many people”. This understanding of disasters frames the causes of death as unusual, unanticipated, and temporally limited. Yet, the deaths of persons crossing borders, especially those crossing in ways that have been illegalised, and the reality of migrants ‘going missing’ on their journey to Europe have become both routine and a predictable consequence of border securitisation and of state authorities’ deterrence policies and strategies. Indeed, there is extensive scientific research demonstrating that the causes and reasons for migrant deaths and disappearances are largely structural and systemic, made up of social, economic and political policies and institutions. For these reasons, MDVI includes challenges that are different from ‘traditional’ DVI events. These are not limited to scientific or technical challenges—which include, for example, the fact that “many of the accepted methods of identification (DNA; fingerprints; dental) are often inappropriate or even impossible, due to legal obstacles and socioeconomic conditions of the countries of origin and the resulting lack of regular dental treatment, fingerprint resources and family records.” Rather, some of the unique challenges associated with MDVI are structural, arising from both politics and policy. Whilst most technical challenges (and some political ones) have been acknowledged, it must also be acknowledged that the causes of migrant deaths and disappearances are integrally linked with ongoing policies and practices willfully enacted by state authorities to control borders, and systemically deficient state responses to such unlawful acts. In absence of a clear, contextualised safeguarding structure alive to the specificities of ‘migrant disasters’, any steps or interventions taken under the umbrella of MDVI with the intention to improve identification procedures may in fact contribute to further harm—including against the dead and their loved ones, others on the move, and/or support groups. Such harm from identification procedures risks contributing to additional death and disappearance caused by harmful border control policies, and the failure to hold state actions to account. These guiding principles aim to help state-led DVI processes in the migration context adequately account and respond to this potential for ongoing and further harm. The principles build and elaborate on the ethical guidelines that already bind forensic and medical professionals as communities of practice, while seeking to integrate critical reflections on harm arising from lived experiences of border/ing violence and family accompaniment. *** This document is a working draft and an invitation to be in conversation around its substantive content.
